title: Introduction to Normalization
text:
What is Normalization?
Normalization (or Schema Refinement) is a systematic technique of organizing data in a database. It involves decomposing a large, poorly-structured table into smaller, well-structured tables.
Normalization serves two primary purposes:

title: Introduction to Normalization
text:
Functional Dependencies (FDs)
A Functional Dependency, denoted as \(X \rightarrow Y\), means that the attribute(s) \(X\) uniquely determines the attribute(s) \(Y\). If you know the value of \(X\), you can look up exactly one corresponding value of \(Y\).

Example: \(StudentID \rightarrow StudentName\). If you know the ID, there is only one possible name associated with it. Here, \(X\) is called the Determinant.

title: Introduction to Normalization
text:
Database Keys

Superkey: A set of one or more attributes that can uniquely identify a row in a table. If \(\{StudentID\}\) is a superkey, then \(\{StudentID, StudentName\}\) is also a superkey.
Candidate Key: A minimal superkey. It is a superkey where no proper subset of its attributes can uniquely identify a row. There can be multiple candidate keys in a table.
Primary Key: The specific candidate key chosen by the database designer to uniquely identify rows.

title: Introduction to Normalization
text:
Attribute Types
Based on the Candidate Keys, all attributes in a table are divided into two categories:

Prime Attribute: An attribute that is a part of any candidate key.
Non-Prime Attribute: An attribute that is not a part of any candidate key.

title: Normal Forms (1NF to 3NF)
text:
1NF (First Normal Form)
A Normal Form specifies a set of conditions that a relational schema must satisfy in terms of its constraints. As we move from 1NF up to higher normal forms, the rules become stricter, and data redundancy is further reduced.
A relation is in First Normal Form (1NF) if and only if it satisfies the following rules:

title: Normal Forms (1NF to 3NF)
text:
2NF Solved Example
Consider a relation \(R(A, B, C, D, E, F)\) and its Functional Dependencies: \[FD=\{AB \rightarrow CDE, \space E \rightarrow F, \space BF \rightarrow A, \space C \rightarrow B\}\]
Step 1: Find the Candidate Keys Let’s find the closures of attribute sets to see which ones determine all attributes in \(R\).

\((AB)^+ = \{A, B, C, D, E, F\}\)
Since \(C \rightarrow B\), we can substitute \(B\) with \(C\): \((AC)^+ = \{A, C, B, D, E, F\}\)
Since \(BF \rightarrow A\), if we have \(B\) and \(F\), we get \(A\). Thus \((BF)^+ = \{B, F, A, C, D, E\}\)

Our Candidate Keys are: \(\{A, B\}, \{A, C\}, \{B, F\}\).
Step 2: Identify Prime and Non-Prime Attributes

Prime Attributes: \(A, B, C, F\) (since they appear in at least one candidate key).
Non-Prime Attributes: \(D, E\).

Step 3: Check for Partial Dependencies We need to check if any non-prime attribute (\(D\) or \(E\)) depends on a proper subset of a candidate key. The proper subsets of our candidate keys are \(\{A\}, \{B\}, \{C\}, \{F\}\).

Do we have \(A \rightarrow D\) or \(A \rightarrow E\)? No.
Do we have \(B \rightarrow D\) or \(B \rightarrow E\)? No.
Do we have \(C \rightarrow D\) or \(C \rightarrow E\)? No (\(C\) only determines \(B\), which is a prime attribute).
Do we have \(F \rightarrow D\) or \(F \rightarrow E\)? No.

Since no non-prime attribute depends on a part of a candidate key, there is no partial dependency. Conclusion: Relation \(R\) is in 2NF.

title: Normal Forms (1NF to 3NF)
text:
3NF Solved Example
Let’s use the same relation \(R(A, B, C, D, E, F)\) with \(FD=\{AB \rightarrow CDE, \space E \rightarrow F, \space BF \rightarrow A, \space C \rightarrow B\}\). We know it is in 2NF. We know the Candidate Keys are \(\{A, B\}, \{A, C\}, \{B, F\}\), and Prime Attributes are \(A, B, C, F\).
Let’s check each FD against the 3NF rules:

\(AB \rightarrow CDE\): \(AB\) is a superkey. (Condition 2 holds - Passes).
\(E \rightarrow F\): \(E\) is not a superkey. However, \(F\) is a prime attribute! (Condition 3 holds - Passes).
\(BF \rightarrow A\): \(BF\) is a superkey. (Condition 2 holds - Passes).
\(C \rightarrow B\): \(C\) is not a superkey. However, \(B\) is a prime attribute! (Condition 3 holds - Passes).

Conclusion: Since every functional dependency satisfies at least one of the 3NF conditions, the relation \(R\) is in 3NF.

title: BCNF and Multivalued Dependencies
text:
BCNF (Boyce-Codd Normal Form)
While 3NF is sufficient for most practical database designs, it still allows certain types of anomalies if there are overlapping candidate keys. Boyce-Codd Normal Form (BCNF) was introduced to handle these edge cases by applying a stricter rule.
A relational schema \(R\) is in BCNF if for every non-trivial functional dependency \(A \rightarrow B\) associated with \(R\), the following condition holds: - \(A\) must be a superkey.
Simply put: The left side of every functional dependency must uniquely identify the entire row. The “prime attribute” loophole present in 3NF is removed.

title: BCNF and Multivalued Dependencies
text:
BCNF Solved Example 1: Success
Consider \(R(A, B, C, D)\) and its \(FD=\{A \rightarrow B, \space B \rightarrow C, \space C \rightarrow D, \space D \rightarrow A\}\)
Step 1: Find Candidate Keys

\(A^+ = \{A, B, C, D\}\)
\(B^+ = \{B, C, D, A\}\)
\(C^+ = \{C, D, A, B\}\)
\(D^+ = \{D, A, B, C\}\) Every single attribute is a candidate key (and thus, a superkey).

Step 2: Check BCNF Condition

For \(A \rightarrow B\), \(A\) is a superkey.
For \(B \rightarrow C\), \(B\) is a superkey.
For \(C \rightarrow D\), \(C\) is a superkey.
For \(D \rightarrow A\), \(D\) is a superkey.

Conclusion: All functional dependencies satisfy the BCNF condition. The relation is in BCNF.

title: BCNF and Multivalued Dependencies
text:
BCNF Solved Example 2: Failure
Let’s look back at the example from the 3NF chapter: \(R(A, B, C, D, E, F)\) with \(FD=\{AB \rightarrow CDE, \space E \rightarrow F, \space BF \rightarrow A, \space C \rightarrow B\}\). We found the candidate keys were \(\{A, B\}, \{A, C\}, \{B, F\}\).
Now let’s check the FDs against the strict BCNF rule:

\(E \rightarrow F\): Is \(E\) a superkey? No.
\(C \rightarrow B\): Is \(C\) a superkey? No.

Conclusion: Because \(E\) and \(C\) are not superkeys, the relation fails BCNF, even though it was successfully in 3NF!

title: BCNF and Multivalued Dependencies
text:
Visualizing MVD



MVD Example


In this example, an instructor teaches a course, and a course has recommended books.

The instructors for a course are completely independent of the books for a course.
Thus, course_name \(\twoheadrightarrow\) instructor
And course_name \(\twoheadrightarrow\) {book, edition}

If you try to store this in a single table, you must repeat every instructor for every book, causing massive data redundancy!

text:
Trivial MVD
An MVD \(X \twoheadrightarrow Y\) is considered trivial if:

\(Y\) is a subset of \(X\) (\(Y \subseteq X\))
Or, \(X \cup Y = R\) (the entire table)

title: Application Programs and Architecture
text:
Application Programs
Databases don’t exist in isolation, they always live inside an application that users interact with. Database-backed applications show up in almost every corner of modern life, for example, travel, communication, education etc. Despite looking completely different, most are built the same way underneath — they all use an RDBMS and they are all split into three layers.

title: Application Programs and Architecture
text:
The Three-Layer Architecture
Think of it like a restaurant : the waiter takes your order (Presentation), the chef decides how to prepare it (Business Logic), and the pantry stores all the ingredients (Data Access). Each role is distinct, and each has its own concerns.



Three-Layer Architecture



Presentation Layer (Frontend)
This is everything the user actually sees and touches. It collects input and displays results. Within the presentation layer, the most widely used design pattern is Model-View-Controller (MVC):







Component
Role




Model
Represents business data and rules


View
Displays data to the user (depends on device/format)


Controller
Receives user events, invokes model actions, selects the view to return





Business Logic Layer (Middle Layer / Tier 2)
Implements the core functionalities, workflows, and rules of the application (such as authentication, search logic, pricing, payment gateways, and order management). It acts as the bridge that connects the frontend and backend layers.

⚠️ The middle layer hides the database schema from the frontend. The frontend never needs to know which table a piece of data lives in.



Data Access Layer (Backend / Tier 3)
Manages persistent data. It is responsible for handling large volumes of information, ensuring high-speed access, maintaining data security, and interfacing directly with the database system .

title: Application Programs and Architecture
text:
Architecture Classification







Tier
What it looks like




1-Tier
All components (user interface, middleware, and backend database) reside on a single server or platform. This is the simplest and most direct setup


2-Tier
A classic client-server model where the client directly communicates with the database server with no intermediate application logic server.


3-Tier
Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access are separated into three independent layers. This is the de-facto standard for DBMS design.


n-Tier
Extends 3-tier by distributing components across many servers with load balancers, caches, and microservices

title: Application Programs and Architecture
text:
Web Applications and Scripting

The World Wide Web
The Web is a massive collection of hypertext documents (HTML pages) spread across servers worldwide, all linked to each other. HTML can contain text, images, hyperlinks, and forms — input fields that let users send data back to a server, which is the bridge between the user and the database.



URLs, URIs, and URNs
Every resource on the web needs an address. A URL like http://www.acm.org/sigmod has three parts:
http  ://  www.acm.org  /sigmod
 ↑              ↑           ↑
Protocol    Machine name   Document path

URI — An umbrella term that covers both locators (URLs) and names (URNs).
URL — Specifies how to retrieve a resource and where it is located, functioning like a person’s street address.
URN — Serves as a unique identifier for a resource, functioning like a person’s name. It defines the identity of a resource but does not specify its location




HTML and HTTP

HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) : Used to format content, embed links, display tables, and gather user input through interactive forms (including dropdown menus, text boxes, and buttons).
HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) : The primary communication protocol used between web clients and web servers . The key thing to know: HTTP is connectionless — once the server replies, it immediately forgets the conversation ever happened. Every new request is treated as brand new. This keeps server load manageable (imagine maintaining open connections with millions of users at once).




Sessions and Cookies
HTTP being connectionless creates a problem — how does a website remember you’re logged in as you move between pages?
The answer is cookies. Here’s how it works:

On your first visit, the server sends a small identifying token (cookie) to your browser
Your browser stores it and automatically attaches it to every subsequent request
The server reads it, looks it up, and knows exactly who you are

This is how Amazon keeps your cart alive across sessions. Cookies can be permanent (survive browser restarts) or session-only (deleted when you close the tab).

title: Application Programs and Architecture
text:
Scripting
A script is a set of commands embedded in a web page or on the server, executed at runtime. Scripts are what make pages dynamic. Two types:

Client-Side Scripting
Client-side scripts are downloaded directly to the client’s computer and run locally inside the web browser.

Primary Languages : JavaScript, VBScript.
Purpose : Handles immediate user interactions, validates form inputs locally, and updates page visuals without triggering a full page reload (e.g., AJAX technology).
Security Context : To prevent malicious scripts from accessing local hard drives, client-side scripts are executed in a heavily restricted safe-mode sandbox that prevents direct system calls or unauthorized file operations.



Server-Side Scripting
Server-side scripts are executed entirely on the web server before the final HTML is generated and sent back to the client.

Primary Languages : PHP, JSP, ASP, Python, Perl.
Purpose : Simplifies database integration. Developers embed executable logic or database queries directly within HTML files. The server runs these queries, dynamically inserts the results into the HTML, and returns the finished static webpage to the user.
Security Context : Safe and secure. The client never sees the server’s proprietary code or database connection details—only the final, clean HTML output.




Servlets
A Java Servlet is a Java program that lives on a web/application server and handles HTTP requests. The flow:
User submits form
    → HTTP request hits the server
    → Server loads the Servlet
    → Servlet reads parameters, runs SQL via JDBC
    → Servlet writes HTML response
    → Thread closes
Each request gets its own thread, so many users can be served simultaneously.
Session handling in Servlets uses cookies automatically:
request.getSession(true);                      // create session
session.setAttribute("userid", "alice");       // store data
session.getAttribute("userid");                // retrieve later
Servlets run inside application servers like Apache Tomcat, GlassFish, or JBoss.



JSP (Java Server Pages)
Writing HTML entirely through out.println() in a Servlet is painful. JSP lets you write HTML normally and drop Java logic inside <% ... %> tags wherever needed:
<body>
  <% if (request.getParameter("name") == null) { %>
    Hello, World!
  <% } else { %>
    Hello, <%= request.getParameter("name") %>!
  <% } %>
</body>
The server compiles a JSP page into a Servlet the first time it’s requested, so performance is identical — JSP is just much easier to write and maintain.



PHP
PHP works exactly like JSP — embed logic inside HTML, server executes it, client gets plain HTML. It has extensive database libraries (ODBC) and was the dominant language for web development for many years.
<body>
  <?php
    if (!isset($_REQUEST['name'])) { echo "Hello World"; }
    else { echo "Hello, " . $_REQUEST['name']; }
  ?>
</body>
PHP and JSP are conceptually the same. The choice between them comes down to the tech stack being used.

title: SQL and Native Languages
text:
ODBC (Open Database Connectivity)
When an application needs to talk to a database, it uses an API (Application Programming Interface) — a standard set of function calls that let you:
There are two broad approaches to doing this:
ODBC is a standard API that lets applications talk to any database, regardless of which RDBMS is being used. The same Python or C code can connect to MySQL, PostgreSQL, or SQL Server with minimal changes, you just swap the driver.
It was originally developed by Microsoft and works with C, C++, C#, Visual Basic, and Python.
A typical ODBC workflow:

title: SQL and Native Languages
text:
Open a connection to the database
Send a query or update
Fetch results
Close the connection

title: SQL and Native Languages
SQL and Native Languages
text:
Connectionist Bridges
Sometimes the driver you need doesn’t exist — for example, you want to connect a Java app to a database that only has an ODBC driver. Bridges solve this by translating function calls from one standard to another.







Bridge
What it does




JDBC-to-ODBC
JDBC driver internally uses an ODBC driver to reach the database


ODBC-to-JDBC
ODBC driver internally uses a JDBC driver


OLE DB-to-ODBC
Microsoft’s OLE DB provider translated to ODBC calls


ADO.NET-to-ODBC
ADO.NET provider (used in .NET apps) translated to ODBC



Think of a bridge as a translator — it lets two systems that speak different languages work together.

title: SQL and Native Languages
SQL and Native Languages
text:
Connecting Python to PostgreSQL
The most popular Python library for working with PostgreSQL is psycopg2 — it’s stable, actively maintained, thread-safe, and works with both Python 2 and 3.
Install it with:
pip install psycopg2
Every interaction with the database follows the same six steps:







Step
What happens




1. Create connection
psycopg2.connect(...) — opens a connection to the DB


2. Create cursor
conn.cursor() — creates a cursor to execute queries


3. Execute query
cur.execute(sql) — runs your SQL


4. Fetch results
fetchone(), fetchmany(), or fetchall()


5. Commit or rollback
conn.commit() to save, conn.rollback() to undo


6. Close
cur.close() then conn.close()

title: SQL and Native Languages
text:
Key API Methods
Connection:
conn = psycopg2.connect(database="mydb", user="myuser",
                         password="mypass", host="127.0.0.1", port="5432")
conn.commit()    # saves changes
conn.rollback()  # undoes changes since last commit
conn.close()     # closes the connection
Cursor:
cur = conn.cursor()
cur.execute("INSERT INTO employee VALUES (%s, %s)", (id, name))  # parameterized query
cur.rowcount     # number of rows affected by last operation
cur.fetchone()   # returns next row, or None
cur.fetchmany(n) # returns next n rows as a list
cur.fetchall()   # returns all remaining rows as a list
cur.close()

Use %s as a placeholder in queries instead of string formatting — this protects against SQL injection.

title: SQL and Native Languages
text:
CRUD Operations in Python
CREATE table:
cur.execute('''CREATE TABLE EMPLOYEE (
    emp_num  INT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
    emp_name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
    department VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL)''')
conn.commit()
INSERT:
cur.execute("INSERT INTO EMPLOYEE VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", (110, 'Bhaskar', 'HR'))
conn.commit()
UPDATE:
cur.execute("UPDATE EMPLOYEE SET department = %s WHERE emp_num = %s", ('Finance', 110))
conn.commit()
DELETE:
cur.execute("DELETE FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE emp_num = %s", (110,))
conn.commit()
SELECT:
cur.execute("SELECT emp_num, emp_name, department FROM EMPLOYEE")
rows = cur.fetchall()
for row in rows:
    print(row[0], row[1], row[2])

text:
Rapid Application Development (RAD)
Building rich web application interfaces, especially the kind of interactive, dynamic pages we see today takes a lot of effort. RAD is an approach that aims to shorten that development cycle by focusing on fast prototyping, quick feedback, and iterative delivery rather than long planning phases.
The four phases of RAD are:
The key idea: prototypes are built quickly, feedback is collected early, and each iteration gets you closer to the final product.

Data Modeling — design the data structures

Testing & Turnover — test, refine, and deploy

title: RAD, Application Security, and Mobile Apps
text:
Application Performance
Popular web applications can have millions of users, with thousands of requests hitting the server every second at peak times. Serving each request by running a fresh database query every single time would be extremely slow and expensive. Caching is the main tool used to tackle this.

Where Caching Happens







Location
What gets cached




Server — Connection Pool
JDBC connections are kept open and reused across requests instead of opening a new one each time


Server — Query Results
Results of frequent database queries are stored in memory; the DB is only hit again if the underlying data changes


Server — Generated HTML
If a page looks the same for many users, the rendered HTML is cached and served directly


Client Network — Web Proxy
Pages are cached at the network level and served to nearby users without hitting the server



Connection pooling in particular is a big win — opening a new database connection is expensive, so reusing existing ones across requests saves significant time.

title: RAD, Application Security, and Mobile Apps
text:
Application Security
Security is one of the most critical and most commonly overlooked aspects of web application development. Here are the major threats and how to address them.

SQL Injection
This is one of the most common and dangerous attacks. It happens when user input is directly concatenated into a SQL query string without sanitization.
Example of a vulnerable query:
"SELECT * FROM instructor WHERE name = '" + name + "'"
If a user types X' or 'Y' = 'Y as their name, the query becomes:
SELECT * FROM instructor WHERE name = 'X' or 'Y' = 'Y'
This returns every row in the table. A malicious user could even inject:
X'; UPDATE instructor SET salary = salary + 10000; --
The fix — always use prepared statements:
PreparedStatement ps = conn.prepareStatement(
    "SELECT * FROM instructor WHERE name = ?"
);
ps.setString(1, name);
The ? placeholder ensures the input is treated as data, never as SQL code. Special characters get automatically escaped.

⚠️ Note: conn.prepareStatement("SELECT ... WHERE name = '" + name + "'") is not a prepared statement — it’s just a regular string with a misleading name. Always use ? placeholders.



Password Leakage

Never store database passwords in plain text inside script files (.php, .jsp) that live in web-accessible directories.
Web servers execute script files but may accidentally serve backup files (e.g., file.jsp~ or .file.jsp.swp) as raw text, exposing credentials.
Restrict database server access to only the IP addresses of your application servers.



Authentication
Passwords alone are increasingly insufficient — they can be guessed, sniffed, reused across sites, or stolen by spyware.
Two-factor authentication (2FA) adds a second layer: - Password + OTP sent via SMS - Password + a hardware token that generates a new pseudo-random number every minute (both the device and the server compute the same sequence independently)


Application-Level Authorization
Standard SQL authorization works at the table or column level — you can say “this user can read the takes table”, but you can’t say “this student can only see their own rows”. The database has no concept of who the application user is.
Workaround — use views:
CREATE VIEW studentTakes AS
    SELECT * FROM takes
    WHERE takes.ID = syscontext.user_id();
This filters rows based on the currently logged-in user’s identity, which the application passes to the database. It works, but creating a view for every such rule gets unwieldy.


Audit Trails
Every sensitive action in an application should be logged: who accessed what data, who made what change, and when. Audit trails are used after a breach to detect what happened, repair the damage and trace who was responsible.
Logs are needed at both the database level (who ran which queries) and the application level (which user performed which action in the UI).

title: RAD, Application Security, and Mobile Apps
text:
Challenges in Web Application Development
Building a web application involves more than just writing code. The major challenges are:

User Interface & Experience — making interfaces that are intuitive and work across devices
Scalability — handling growth in users and data without redesigning the system
Performance — keeping response times low under heavy load
Framework & Platform Knowledge — choosing and mastering the right tools
Security — protecting against the threats covered above

title: RAD, Application Security, and Mobile Apps
text:
Mobile Apps

What is a Mobile App?
A mobile app is application software designed to run on smartphones and tablets. The key difference from desktop development is the set of constraints the device imposes:



Constraint
Capability




Small screen / form factor
Touchscreen & gesture-based navigation


Limited memory & CPU
Accelerometer, GPS, camera sensors


Limited battery
Always-on connectivity (WiFi, 4G/5G)


Limited bandwidth
Push notifications



Design must account for both the limitations and the unique capabilities.


Architecture of a Mobile App
Mobile apps follow the same 3-tier architecture as web apps — Presentation, Business Logic, and Data Access. The main difference is in the Data layer, which is often split:

Local data — stored on the device (SQLite, cached files) for offline access and speed
Remote data — fetched from a server API when connected

The app also needs to be customized per platform (Android, iOS, Windows), since each has its own OS, UI guidelines, and APIs.


Types of Mobile Apps








Type
How it works
Trade-off




Native
Written in the platform’s own language (Java/Kotlin for Android, Swift/Objective-C for iOS)
Best performance and device integration, but separate codebase per platform


Web App
Runs in a browser using HTML/CSS/JS
Fully portable, but limited access to device features


Hybrid
Wraps a web app in a native shell
One codebase for all platforms, but performance trade-offs

title: Tree Data Structures
text:
Introduction to Trees
In the previous weeks, we explored linear data models and the relational model. As we move deeper into the physical storage and organization of data (especially for indexes), we will frequently encounter Trees.
Unlike arrays or linked lists, a tree is a hierarchical data structure.

title: Tree Data Structures
text:
A visual representation of a binary tree structure.



Understanding Tree Properties
Let’s break down the terminology using the tree above:

Root: The topmost node in the tree.
Internal Nodes: Any node which has at least one child. They act as the “branches”.
Leaf Nodes: Nodes with no children (the endpoints of the tree).
Subtree: A portion of the tree that itself forms a complete tree, rooted at one of the nodes.
Siblings: Nodes that share the exact same parent node.
Arity (or Degree): The number of children a specific node has. The Arity of a Tree is the maximum arity of any node within that tree.
Level / Depth: The distance from the root. The root is at level 0, its children at level 1, and so on.
Height: The maximum level (or depth) in the tree.







TipKey Mathematical Facts about Trees




Edges vs. Nodes: A tree with \(n\) nodes will always have exactly \(n-1\) edges.
Maximum nodes at a level: The maximum number of nodes at level \(l\) of a binary tree is \(2^l\).
Maximum nodes by height: The maximum number of nodes in a binary tree of height \(h\) is \(2^{h+1} - 1\).

title: Tree Data Structures
text:
Binary Search Trees (BST)
A Binary Search Tree is a special type of binary tree that maintains a strict ordering property, making searching incredibly efficient.






ImportantThe BST Property



For every node in a Binary Search Tree: - All values in the left subtree are strictly less than the node’s value. - All values in the right subtree are strictly greater than the node’s value.



Step-by-Step Construction
Let’s build a BST from the following sequence of data: 17, 22, 12, 10, 14, 25, 19.
Imagine inserting these numbers one by one:

Insert 17: This is our first number, so it becomes the Root.
Insert 22: We compare 22 with 17. Since \(22 > 17\), it goes to the right.
Insert 12: Compare 12 with 17. Since \(12 < 17\), it goes to the left.
Insert 10: Compare 10 with 17 (left), then compare with 12. Since \(10 < 12\), it goes to the left of 12.
Insert 14: Compare 14 with 17 (left), then compare with 12. Since \(14 > 12\), it goes to the right of 12.
Insert 25: Compare 25 with 17 (right), then compare with 22. Since \(25 > 22\), it goes to the right of 22.
Insert 19: Compare 19 with 17 (right), then compare with 22. Since \(19 < 22\), it goes to the left of 22.

The final result is the beautiful structure shown below!



The fully constructed Binary Search Tree.


Notice how you can pick any node (like 22), and instantly see that its left child (19) is smaller and its right child (25) is larger. This property allows us to search for any number in \(O(\log n)\) time on average, which is foundational for database indexes.

title: Storage Hierarchy
text:
Physical Storage Media
Data needs a place to live! Depending on how fast we need to access the data and how long we want it to survive without power, we use different types of storage media.
There is a fundamental divide in storage media: Volatile vs. Non-Volatile.

title: Storage Hierarchy
text:
NoteVolatile Storage



Volatile storage devices lose all their data when the power is interrupted or turned off.

Primary characteristic: Extremely fast but temporary.
Examples: Cache Memory, Random Access Memory (RAM).









NoteNon-Volatile Storage



Non-volatile storage devices retain their data regardless of whether the power is on or off.

Primary characteristic: Slower than volatile storage, but permanent (until deleted).
Examples: Hard Disk Drives (HDD), Solid State Drives (SSD), Pen Drives, Magnetic Tapes.

title: Storage Hierarchy
text:
The Storage Hierarchy Pyramid
In computer architecture, we can’t build a single storage device that is infinitely fast, infinitely large, and extremely cheap. We have to make trade-offs.

If you want speed, it costs more and you get less capacity.
If you want capacity, it costs less per gigabyte, but you sacrifice speed.

This trade-off creates the Storage Hierarchy.





graph TD
    classDef volatile fill:#f9d0c4,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef nonvolatile fill:#d4edda,stroke:#333,stroke-width:2px;

    subgraph Speed_vs_Capacity [ ]
    direction BT
    L1[Registers]:::volatile
    L2[Cache]:::volatile
    L3[Main Memory / RAM]:::volatile
    L4[Flash Memory / SSD]:::nonvolatile
    L5[Magnetic Disks / HDD]:::nonvolatile
    L6[Magnetic Tapes / Optical Disks]:::nonvolatile
    
    L6 --> L5 --> L4 --> L3 --> L2 --> L1
    end







Breaking Down the Layers

Primary Storage (Top 3 layers):

Registers & Cache: The fastest and most costly forms of storage. Cache is managed by the computer hardware to hold frequently accessed data close to the CPU.
Main Memory (RAM): Very fast, but volatile. When your database is running, the active queries and data are held here for immediate processing.

Secondary Storage:

Flash Memory (SSDs) & Magnetic Disks (HDDs): Moderately fast and non-volatile. This is where your entire database is permanently stored. When a query is made, data is fetched from here and moved into Main Memory.

Tertiary Storage:

Magnetic Tapes & Optical Disks: Very slow and non-volatile. They offer massive capacity for extremely cheap prices. They are primarily used for archival backups (e.g., storing 10 years of historical data that is rarely accessed).

title: Disk Performance Math
text:
Intuition Behind the Math
Memorizing formulas can be difficult. It is much easier if we understand why the formulas exist. Let’s look at the basic math behind disk performance.

title: Disk Performance Math
text:
1. Capacity of a Disk
How much data can a disk hold? Imagine you have a bookshelf. The capacity of the shelf is the number of books it holds times the pages in one book. Similarly, a disk is made of sectors. \[Capacity = Total \ No. \ of \ Sectors \times Size \ of \ One \ Sector\]


2. Time Period of One Rotation
If a disk spins at \(RPM\) (Revolutions Per Minute), how long does one single rotation take? If it does \(RPM\) revolutions in 60,000 milliseconds (1 minute), then one revolution takes: \[Time \ Period = \frac{1 \ minute}{RPM} = \frac{60,000 \ ms}{RPM}\]


3. Transfer Rate
How much data can we read per unit of time? In one single rotation (Time Period), the head sweeps over an entire track. Therefore, the data transferred in one rotation is exactly the capacity of one track. \[Transfer \ Rate = \frac{Bytes \ on \ one \ Track}{Time \ Period}\]


4. Transfer Time
If we know our speed (Transfer Rate) and the distance we need to cover (File Size), we can find the time! This is just \(Time = Distance \div Speed\). \[Transfer \ Time = \frac{File \ Size}{Transfer \ Rate}\]


5. Addressing Sectors
Every sector needs a unique ID (binary address) so the OS can find it. If you have 8 sectors, you need 3 bits to address them (\(000\) to \(111\)). This is because \(2^3 = 8\). To find the number of bits required for \(N\) sectors, we take the base-2 logarithm. \[Minimum \ Bits = \lceil \log_2(Total \ No. \ of \ Sectors) \rceil\] (We use the ceiling function \(\lceil \rceil\) because we can’t have a fraction of a bit).

title: Disk Performance Math
text:
Solved Examples
Let’s put our intuition to work with some structured numerical problems.






ImportantSolved Example 1: Reading a File



Problem Statement: Consider you have a file named “IITM BSc” in your hard disk. The file size is 1000 KB. Seek time of your hard disk read head is 3ms, rotational speed is 30,000 RPM. The disk has 200 sectors/track and sector size is 512 bytes.

What is the transfer rate of your hard-disk (in KB/ms)?
Considering the fact that the file data is stored in all non-consecutive sectors, how much time will be required to read the whole file after the read request is made? (Note: Consider Access time + Transfer time)

Part A: Finding the Transfer Rate

Given:

\(RPM = 30,000\)
\(Sectors \ per \ Track = 200\)
\(Sector \ Size = 512 \ Bytes\)

Step-by-step Solution:

First, find the Time Period for one rotation: \(Time \ Period = \frac{60,000 \ ms}{30,000} = 2 \ ms\)
Second, find the capacity of one track (Bytes on one track): \(Track \ Capacity = 200 \ sectors \times 512 \ bytes = 102,400 \ Bytes = 100 \ KB\) (Note: we assume \(1024 \ Bytes = 1 \ KB\))
Finally, calculate Transfer Rate: \(Transfer \ Rate = \frac{100 \ KB}{2 \ ms} = \mathbf{50 \ KB/ms}\)


Part B: Finding Total Read Time (Non-Consecutive Sectors)

Given:

\(File \ Size = 1000 \ KB\)
\(Seek \ Time = 3 \ ms\)
Data is stored in non-consecutive sectors. This is a critical detail! It means for every single sector we read, we have to suffer Seek Time and Rotational Latency!

Step-by-step Solution:

First, find the total number of sectors the file occupies: \(File \ Size \ in \ Bytes = 1000 \ KB \times 1024 = 1,024,000 \ Bytes\) \(Number \ of \ Sectors = \frac{1,024,000 \ Bytes}{512 \ Bytes} = 2000 \ Sectors\)
Next, find the Access Time for one sector: \(Average \ Rotational \ Latency = \frac{1}{2} \times Time \ Period = \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \ ms = 1 \ ms\) \(Access \ Time = Seek \ Time + Rotational \ Latency = 3 \ ms + 1 \ ms = 4 \ ms\)
Next, find the Transfer Time for one sector: \(Transfer \ Time \ (1 \ Sector) = \frac{Sector \ Size}{Transfer \ Rate} = \frac{0.5 \ KB}{50 \ KB/ms} = 0.01 \ ms\)
Finally, calculate the total time for all 2000 non-consecutive sectors: \(Time \ per \ Sector = Access \ Time + Transfer \ Time = 4 \ ms + 0.01 \ ms = 4.01 \ ms\) \(Total \ Time = 2000 \times 4.01 \ ms = \mathbf{8020 \ ms}\) (or 8.02 seconds)











ImportantSolved Example 2: Disk Geometry and Addressing



Problem Statement: Consider a disk with 10 platters, 64 tracks/surface, 256 sectors/track, 512 bytes/sector. 4 bytes/sector is reserved for storing file system information (formatting data).

How much free space is available for use (in MB, upto two decimal places)?
How many bits are required for addressing all the sectors?

Part A: Finding Free Space

Given:

\(Platters = 10\) (Note: A platter has 2 surfaces! So \(Surfaces = 20\))
\(Tracks \ per \ Surface = 64\)
\(Sectors \ per \ Track = 256\)
\(Sector \ Size = 512 \ Bytes\)
\(Reserved \ Space = 4 \ Bytes / sector\)

Step-by-step Solution:

First, find the total number of sectors on the entire disk: \(Total \ Sectors = Surfaces \times Tracks/Surface \times Sectors/Track\) \(Total \ Sectors = 20 \times 64 \times 256 = 327,680 \ Sectors\)
Next, calculate the usable space per sector: \(Usable \ Sector \ Size = 512 - 4 = 508 \ Bytes\)
Finally, calculate the total free space: \(Total \ Free \ Space = 327,680 \times 508 \ Bytes = 166,461,440 \ Bytes\) Convert to MB (divide by \(1024^2\)): \(Free \ Space \ in \ MB = \frac{166,461,440}{1,048,576} \approx \mathbf{158.75 \ MB}\)


Part B: Addressing Sectors

Step-by-step Solution:

We know there are \(327,680\) total sectors on the disk.
We apply the addressing formula: \(Minimum \ Bits = \lceil \log_2(327,680) \rceil\) Since \(2^{18} = 262,144\) and \(2^{19} = 524,288\), we know we need more than 18 bits. \(Minimum \ Bits = \mathbf{19 \ bits}\)

title: Algorithms & Data Structures
text: Algorithms and Complexity Analysis

title: Algorithms & Data Structures
text:
Basics and Definitions

Algorithm vs. Program: An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined, computer-implementable instructions to solve a class of problems or to perform a computation. Crucially, an algorithm must terminate. A program, such as an operating system, is an implementation that may run indefinitely without terminating.



Motivation for Analysis
Why do we analyze algorithms? - To predict performance (how fast will this run on a billion rows?). - To avoid bugs and provide guarantees on execution boundaries. - To understand the theoretical limits of computational problems.


Factors of Analysis
When we analyze an algorithm, we measure the “cost” based on several factors:

Time Complexity: How long does it take to execute?
Space/Storage Complexity: How much memory (RAM) does it consume?
Other factors: Power consumption and network bandwidth (especially relevant in cloud databases).



Methodologies

Counting Model: A simplified theoretical model (Random-Access Machine) where we sum the cost and frequency of primitive operations (like addition, assignment, etc.).
Asymptotic Analysis: We use Big-Oh (\(O\)) notation to measure the growth of resource requirements as the input size (\(n\)) increases toward infinity. We typically focus on the Worst case and Average case scenarios.


Complexity Classes
From fastest (best) to slowest (worst):

\(O(1)\) - Constant Time
\(O(\log n)\) - Logarithmic Time
\(O(n)\) - Linear Time
\(O(n \log n)\) - Linearithmic Time
\(O(n^2)\) - Quadratic Time
\(O(n^3)\) - Cubic Time
\(O(2^n)\) - Exponential Time

title: Algorithms & Data Structures
text:
Data Structures
A Data Structure is a specialized format for organizing, processing, retrieving and storing data in memory. Standard operations on any data structure include: Create, Insert, Delete, Find (Search), Update, and Close.

Linear Data Structures

Arrays: Contiguous blocks of memory.

Advantage: Extremely fast indexed/random access (\(O(1)\)).
Disadvantage: Very slow insertion/deletion (\(O(n)\)) because all subsequent elements must be shifted.

Linked Lists: Elements are stored in nodes that contain pointers to the next node.

Advantage: Very fast insertion/deletion (\(O(1)\) if you are already at the position).
Disadvantage: Slow sequential access (\(O(n)\)) since you must traverse from the head.

Queues: Follow First-In-First-Out (FIFO) logic (like a line at a grocery store).
Stacks: Follow Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) logic (like a stack of plates).

title: Algorithms & Data Structures
text:
Non-Linear Data Structures: Trees
Unlike arrays or linked lists, a tree is a hierarchical data structure. They are absolutely critical for database indexing.



A visual representation of a binary tree structure.


Let’s break down the terminology:

Root: The topmost node.
Parent/Child: A node connected to nodes directly below it is a parent.
Leaf Nodes: Nodes with no children.
Arity (or Degree): The number of children a specific node has.
Level / Depth: The distance from the root.
Height: The maximum level in the tree.


Binary Search Trees (BST)
A Binary Search Tree maintains a strict ordering property. For every node, all values in the left subtree are strictly less than the node’s value, and all values in the right subtree are greater.
Let’s build a BST from the data: 17, 22, 12, 10, 14, 25, 19.

Insert 17: This is our first number, so it becomes the Root.
Insert 22: We compare 22 with 17. Since \(22 > 17\), it goes to the right.
Insert 12: Compare 12 with 17. Since \(12 < 17\), it goes to the left.
Insert 10: Compare 10 with 17 (left), then compare with 12. Since \(10 < 12\), it goes to the left of 12. … and so on.

The final result is the beautiful structure shown below!



The fully constructed Binary Search Tree.


If the tree remains balanced, this property allows us to search, insert, and delete in \(O(\log n)\) time, making it immensely faster than scanning an array.

title: Algorithms & Data Structures
text:
Search and Sorting

Linear Search: Sequential checking of every element. Complexity is \(O(n)\).
Binary Search: An extremely efficient search on sorted arrays (or Binary Search Trees). At each step, it halves the search space. Complexity is \(O(\log n)\).
Sorting Algorithms: Common algorithms to organize data include Quicksort (\(O(n \log n)\)), Mergesort (\(O(n \log n)\)), Heap Sort (\(O(n \log n)\)), and the much slower Insertion Sort (\(O(n^2)\)).

title: Physical Storage Systems
text:
Physical Storage Media
Data needs a place to live! Depending on how fast we need to access the data and how long we want it to survive without power, we use different types of storage media.
There is a fundamental divide in storage media: Volatile vs. Non-Volatile.

title: Physical Storage Systems
text:
Volatile Storage: Loses all data when the power is interrupted (e.g., Cache Memory, Main Memory / RAM). Extremely fast but temporary.
Non-Volatile Storage: Retains data regardless of power status (e.g., Flash memory, Magnetic Disks, Optical Disks, Magnetic Tapes). Slower, but permanent.


The Storage Hierarchy Pyramid
In computer architecture, we make trade-offs. If you want speed, it costs more and you get less capacity. If you want capacity, it costs less per gigabyte, but you sacrifice speed.

title: Physical Storage Systems
text:
Inside a Magnetic Disk (HDD)
To understand database performance, we must look at the physical mechanics of where our data actually lives: Magnetic Disks.



The inside of a typical magnetic disk.


Think of a hard drive like an old-school vinyl record player:

Platter (The Record): The circular disk coated with magnetic material.
Spindle (The Turntable Motor): The central rod that spins the platters at high speeds (e.g., 7200 RPM).
Read/Write Head (The Needle): The tiny magnet that hovers above the platter.
Actuator Arm (The Tonearm): The mechanical arm that moves the Read/Write head.


Data Organization on the Disk



A breakdown of disk geometry.



(A) Track: A single, concentric circular ring on the surface of the platter.
(C) Sector: A track is divided into smaller arcs called sectors. It is the smallest unit of data that can be read or written (traditionally 512 bytes).
Cylinder: The set of all tracks that are at the exact same position across all stacked platters.
(D) Block / Cluster: A grouping of contiguous sectors used by the operating system to allocate space efficiently.

title: Physical Storage Systems
text:
Disk Performance Metrics
When a database asks the hard drive for a piece of data, the mechanical parts have to move.

1. Access Time
The total time it takes to begin reading the actual data. \[Access \ Time = Seek \ Time + Rotational \ Latency\]

Seek Time: The time taken to physically reposition the arm over the correct track.
Rotational Latency: The time spent waiting for the correct sector to rotate directly underneath the head.



2. Data Transfer Rate
The speed at which data is moved from the disk to the main memory once the head is in position.


3. Reliability (MTTF)
Hard drives are mechanical, which means they will eventually break. Reliability is measured by Mean Time To Failure (MTTF). An MTTF of 5 years doesn’t mean it will break in exactly 5 years, but it provides a statistical average of expected lifespan.

title: Physical Storage Systems
text:
Emerging Technologies
While Magnetic Disks are still widely used, new technologies are constantly evolving storage:

Solid State Drives (SSD): Use flash memory to store data persistently without any moving parts, significantly reducing Access Time.
Cloud Storage: Abstracting the physical hardware entirely, relying on distributed remote servers.
DNA Digital Storage: A futuristic approach using synthetic DNA to store massive amounts of data with extreme longevity.
Quantum Memory: Theoretical storage systems leveraging quantum states for unprecedented speeds and security.

title: Disk Performance Math
text:
Intuition Behind the Math
Memorizing formulas can be difficult. It is much easier if we understand why the formulas exist. Let’s look at the basic math behind disk performance.

title: Disk Performance Math
text:
1. Capacity of a Disk
How much data can a disk hold? Imagine you have a bookshelf. The capacity of the shelf is the number of books it holds times the pages in one book. Similarly, a disk is made of sectors. \[Capacity = Total \ No. \ of \ Sectors \times Size \ of \ One \ Sector\]

title: File Organization & Buffering
text:
File Structure and Organization
Before we can query a database, the raw data must be mapped onto the physical disk blocks we discussed in the previous chapters.

title: File Organization & Buffering
text:
The Data Hierarchy

Database: The highest level, containing multiple files.
File: A collection of related records (e.g., the Instructor table).
Record: A single instance of data (e.g., a specific instructor’s row).
Field / Attribute: The individual data points within a record (e.g., Name, Salary).



Record Management

Fixed-length Records: Every record takes up the exact same amount of space. This makes math easy, but deletions leave “holes”. These are managed via periodic compaction, shifting records, or using a “Free List” to track empty spaces.
Variable-length Records: Used when attributes vary in size (like VARCHAR). These are much harder to manage and usually require storing offsets and using Slotted Pages to organize the data block dynamically.



File Organization Types
How do we arrange these records inside a file?

Heap Organization: Records are placed wherever there is free space. Completely unordered.
Sequential Organization: Records are strictly ordered by a “Search Key” (like ordering a dictionary alphabetically). Excellent for sequential processing.
Multi-table Clustering: Purposely grouping related records from different tables (e.g., a Department record physically stored right next to all its Instructor records) into the same disk block. This minimizes expensive disk I/O when performing SQL JOIN operations.

Note: The Data Dictionary (System Catalog) is a special file that stores metadata—data about the data itself! It tracks schemas, users, and integrity constraints.

title: File Organization & Buffering
text:
Storage Access and Buffer Management
We’ve established a crucial fact: Disks are slow, but Main Memory (RAM) is fast. Every time the database needs to read or write a record, it must transfer an entire Block of data between the disk and main memory. This disk I/O is the biggest bottleneck in database performance.
Enter the Buffer Manager.

The Role of the Buffer Manager
The Buffer Manager is a software subsystem responsible for allocating space in main memory to temporarily hold blocks fetched from the disk.
When a query requests data:

The Buffer Manager checks if the required block is already in the buffer (Main Memory).
If YES, this is a “Cache Hit”. The data is served instantly.
If NO, this is a “Cache Miss”. The Buffer Manager must fetch the block from the slow magnetic disk.



Replacement Policies
If the buffer is completely full of blocks, and we need to fetch a new one from the disk, which old block should we evict (throw out) to make room? This is determined by a Replacement Policy.






TipLeast Recently Used (LRU)



The most common strategy. The Buffer Manager evicts the block that hasn’t been accessed for the longest time.
Intuition: If you haven’t looked at a block in a long time, you probably won’t need it again soon.








ImportantMost Recently Used (MRU)



Sometimes LRU is a terrible idea! Consider a query using a Nested Loop Join where we repeatedly scan the same large relation (e.g., scanning the entire Instructor table for every single row in the Department table).
If the Instructor table is larger than our buffer, LRU will evict the beginning of the table just before we need to scan it again! In this specific scenario, Most Recently Used (MRU) is better. We evict the block we just finished reading, because in a looping scan, we won’t need it again until the next full loop.




Pinned Blocks
Some operations are so critical that a block cannot be evicted under any circumstances, even if it’s the LRU or MRU. For example, if a block is currently being actively updated by a transaction, the Buffer Manager will Pin the block, restricting it from being written back to disk prematurely.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Why Do We Need Indexes?
Imagine a library with a million books stored in no particular order. Finding a specific title means scanning every shelf — that is linear search, and it is painfully slow for large collections.
A database index solves exactly this problem. It is a separate, smaller data structure that maps search-key values to the actual records in the main table. Think of it like the index at the back of a textbook: you look up a keyword, get the page number, and jump straight there — no full scan needed.
The attribute (or set of attributes) you build the index on is called the search key. An index entry looks like this:
There are two broad families of indexes:
This lecture focuses on ordered indices.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
💡 Key insight: An index file is typically much smaller than the main data file, so searching the index is fast, and then the pointer takes you directly to the right record.





search-key
pointer




“Physics”
→ record #5





Ordered indices — entries are sorted on the search key (like an alphabetical index)
Hash indices — entries are scattered into buckets by a hash function (faster for exact lookups, but can’t handle range queries well)

title: Indexing and Hashing
section: How Do We Judge an Index?
text:
How Do We Judge an Index?
Not all indexes are equally useful. We evaluate them on four metrics:







Metric
What it asks




Access types
Can it handle point lookups and range queries efficiently?


Access time
How fast can we find a record?


Insertion/Deletion time
How much overhead does updating the index add?


Space overhead
How much extra storage does the index consume?



A good index strikes the right balance — fast lookups without ballooning storage or making every insert a nightmare.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Ordered Indices
In an ordered index, entries are sorted on the search key value — exactly like an author catalog in a library. Two important variants:

Primary index (clustering index): The index whose search key matches the physical order of the data file itself. If your Employee table is stored sorted by emp_id, then an index on emp_id is the primary index. Sequential scans using this index are very efficient because records physically adjacent on disk are also logically adjacent.
Secondary index (non-clustering index): An index on a different attribute — say, salary — while the file is still physically ordered by emp_id. The salary values in the index point all over the disk, so a sequential scan through this index is much more expensive (each lookup may fetch a fresh disk block).


⚠️ A table can have only one primary index (since the data has only one physical order) but many secondary indices.

An index-sequential file is the combination: a sequentially ordered file together with its primary index. This is sometimes called ISAM (Indexed Sequential Access Method).

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Dense vs. Sparse Indexes

Dense Index
A dense index has one index entry for every record in the data file.
Think of it as a full directory: every employee gets a line in the lookup table.
Index entry for emp_id = 101  →  record 1
Index entry for emp_id = 102  →  record 2
Index entry for emp_id = 103  →  record 3
...
Advantage: You can tell immediately from the index whether a record exists — no need to visit the data file at all for existence checks.
Disadvantage: The index can grow quite large.



Sparse Index
A sparse index has index entries for only some search-key values — typically one per disk block (or one per group of records).
Index entry for emp_id = 101  →  block 0  (covers records 101–200)
Index entry for emp_id = 201  →  block 1  (covers records 201–300)
...
To find a record with key \(K\): 1. Find the largest index entry with key \(< K\). 2. Follow its pointer to the data block. 3. Scan sequentially within that block until you find \(K\).
Advantage: Much smaller index — fewer entries to store and maintain.
Disadvantage: Slightly slower lookup since you have to scan within a block.

💡 Sweet spot: A sparse index with one entry per disk block is the standard recommended trade-off — small enough to fit in memory, yet granular enough to eliminate most of the sequential scan.

Multilevel Index
Here’s a practical problem: what if the primary index itself is too large to fit in main memory? Searching it becomes expensive again.
The solution is to layer another sparse index on top:

Inner index — the original primary index (on disk)
Outer index — a sparse index built on the inner index (small enough for memory)

Lookup: search the outer index (in memory) → jump to the right block of the inner index → follow the pointer to the actual data.
If even the outer index is too large, add yet another level. This idea of layering sparse indexes is exactly where B-trees come from — which we will cover in the next section.

⚠️ Indices at all levels must be updated whenever the data file changes.

On Insertion

Dense index: look up the key; if absent, insert a new entry in sorted order.
Sparse index: no change needed unless a new disk block is created. If a new block is created, insert an entry for the first key in that new block.

section: Balanced Binary Search Trees: A Recap
text:
Balanced Binary Search Trees: A Recap
Before we can understand the tree structures databases use internally, it helps to revisit the classic Binary Search Tree (BST) and why “balance” matters so much.

Search Complexity Depends on Height
In a BST with \(n\) nodes, search costs \(O(h)\) where \(h\) is the tree’s height.

Best case (balanced): \(h \sim O(\log n)\) — perfect, this is what we want.
Worst case (skewed): \(h = n - 1\) — this happens when keys are inserted in sorted order. The tree degenerates into a linked list, and search becomes \(O(n)\).

Sorted insertion: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Resulting "tree":
  1
   \
    2
     \
      3  ← just a linked list, O(n) search


Keeping It Balanced
A BST is balanced if \(h \sim O(\log n)\). This can be guaranteed by:

AVL Tree: After every insert, check if any node’s left and right subtree heights differ by more than 1. If so, perform a rotation to restore balance. Named after inventors Adelson-Velsky and Landis.
Randomized BST: Insert keys in a uniformly random order — on average, the tree stays balanced without explicit rebalancing.
Skip List: A probabilistic layered structure of sorted linked lists, effectively giving \(O(\log n)\) expected performance.
Splay Tree: A self-adjusting BST that moves recently accessed elements to the root, giving good amortized performance for repeated lookups.

All of these achieve \(O(\log n)\) for search, insert, and delete. But they share a critical limitation:

⚠️ Balanced BSTs work brilliantly in memory but do not scale to external storage (disk). Each node access is a separate disk read, and with \(O(\log n)\) levels, that’s \(O(\log n)\) disk reads — each taking 5–10 milliseconds. For a million records, that’s painfully slow.

This is why databases need a different kind of tree.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
The 2-3-4 Tree: Motivation
The problem with BSTs on disk is that each node holds only one key and has only two children. The tree must be very tall (\(O(\log n)\) levels) to hold \(n\) records.
What if we could make each node fatter — storing multiple keys and having multiple children? Then the tree would be much shorter, and we’d need far fewer disk reads to reach any record.
This idea leads to the 2-3-4 Tree (and ultimately to B-trees, the actual structure used in most database engines).

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
What Is a 2-3-4 Tree?
A 2-3-4 Tree is a balanced search tree where every node can hold 1, 2, or 3 keys (and correspondingly have 2, 3, or 4 children). That is where the name comes from.
The three node types:









Node type
Keys stored
Children
Search key rule




2-node
1 (call it S)
2
left child < S; right child > S


3-node
2 (S and L)
3
left < S; middle: S–L; right > L


4-node
3 (S, M, L)
4
left < S; second: S–M; third: M–L; right > L



A leaf node can hold 1, 2, or 3 data items.
Key properties: - All leaves sit at the same depth — the tree is always perfectly height-balanced. - \(h \sim O(\log n)\), so search, insert, and delete all cost \(O(\log n)\). - Data is always kept in sorted order. - The structure generalizes to larger nodes — the B-tree is exactly this idea extended to nodes with hundreds of children.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Search in a 2-3-4 Tree
Search is a straightforward extension of BST search. At each node, compare the target key against the node’s keys and follow the appropriate child pointer. Repeat until you reach a leaf or find the key.

💡 Because all leaves are at the same depth, every search takes exactly \(O(h) = O(\log n)\) steps — no worst-case skew possible.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Insertion in a 2-3-4 Tree
Insertion always happens at a leaf. The process:

Search for the expected location (the leaf where the key would go).
If the leaf is a 2-node, expand it to a 3-node and insert. Done.
If the leaf is a 3-node, expand it to a 4-node and insert. Done.
If the leaf is a 4-node, we can’t add another key — we must split it first.


Node Splitting
Splitting a 4-node takes its middle key (M) and pushes it up to the parent. The original 4-node becomes two 2-nodes (one holding S, one holding L), both children of the parent which now absorbs M.
There are three cases depending on the parent:
Case 1 — Parent is the root (a 4-node):
    [S  M  L]          [M]
   /  |  |  \    →    /   \
  a   b  c   d      [S]   [L]
                   / \   / \
                  a   b c   d
The tree grows one level taller.
Case 2 — Parent is a 2-node:
The middle key M is absorbed into the parent, converting it from a 2-node to a 3-node. The split 4-node’s two halves (S and L) become two separate children.
Case 3 — Parent is a 3-node:
Same idea — M is absorbed, converting the parent from a 3-node to a 4-node.


Early vs. Late Splitting
There are two strategies for when to split:

Early splitting: Split any 4-node you encounter on the way down during a search, before you actually need to. This ensures you never have a full node at the insertion point. At most one split per level.
Late splitting: Only split when you actually need to insert into a 4-node. May cascade up \(O(h)\) splits in the worst case.

Both strategies produce valid trees with the same complexity \(O(h)\), but they produce different final shapes. The slides follow the early splitting strategy.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Insertion Example: Step by Step
Inserting the sequence 10, 30, 60, 20, 50, 40, 70, 80, 15, 90, 100 using the early splitting strategy.

After inserting 10, 30, 60 — all three fit into one leaf (a 4-node):
[10  30  60]

Insert 20 — the root is a 4-node, so we split it before descending. Middle key 30 becomes the new root; 10 and 60 become separate children. Then 20 is inserted into the left child:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [60]

Insert 50 — 50 > 30, go right. [60] is a 2-node, so just expand it:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [50, 60]

Insert 40 — 40 > 30, go right. [50, 60] is a 3-node, expand to 4-node and insert:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [40, 50, 60]

Insert 70 — root [30] is fine. 70 > 30, descend right. [40, 50, 60] is a 4-node — split it immediately (early strategy). Middle key 50 rises to join the root:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60]
Now insert 70 into the right child [60]:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60, 70]

Insert 80 — 80 > 50, go to right child [60, 70]. It’s a 3-node, expand it:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60, 70, 80]

Insert 15 — 15 < 30, go left. [10, 20] is a 3-node, expand it:
              [30, 50]
             /   |    \
  [10, 15, 20]  [40]  [60, 70, 80]

Insert 90 — root [30, 50] is fine. 90 > 50, descend right. [60, 70, 80] is a 4-node — split it. Middle key 70 rises to join the root:
                [30, 50, 70]
               /   |    |   \
  [10,15,20]  [40] [60] [80]
Now insert 90 into the rightmost child [80]:
                [30, 50, 70]
               /   |    |   \
  [10,15,20]  [40] [60] [80, 90]

Insert 100 — root [30, 50, 70] is a 4-node — split it first. Middle key 50 becomes the new root; 30 and 70 become children:
                      [50]
                     /    \
                  [30]    [70]
                 /    \   /   \
          [10,15,20] [40] [60] [80,90]
Now insert 100. 100 > 50 → go right to [70]. 100 > 70 → go to right child [80, 90]. It’s a 3-node, expand it:
                      [50]
                     /    \
                  [30]    [70]
                 /    \   /   \
          [10,15,20] [40] [60] [80, 90, 100]

Final tree after all 11 insertions:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [30]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [40][60] [80,90,100]
Height = 2. All 11 keys stored, all leaves at the same level. A plain BST with this input could have ended up with height 10 — the 2-3-4 tree keeps it to 2.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Deletion in a 2-3-4 Tree
Deletion is the reverse of insertion. The core idea:

Locate the node containing the target key.
Swap it with its inorder successor (the smallest key in the right subtree). This reduces deletion to always happening at a leaf.
If the leaf is a 3-node or 4-node, simply remove the key.
If the leaf is a 2-node, removing its only key would leave an empty node — which is illegal. To prevent this, transform every 2-node you encounter (on the way down) into a 3-node or 4-node first. This is the reverse of the splitting cases from insertion.


Deletion Example
We will delete 30 and then 50 from the final tree above.
Starting tree:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [30]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [40][60] [80,90,100]

Delete 30
30 is an internal node. Its inorder successor is 40 (smallest key in its right subtree). Swap 30 and 40:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [30][60] [80,90,100]
Now delete 30 from the leaf [30]. That leaf is a 2-node — but since 30 is the only key, removing it would leave an empty node.
However, looking at its sibling [10, 15, 20] (a 4-node), we can borrow from it. The sibling’s largest key (20) rotates up to the parent, and the parent’s key (40) rotates down to fill the now-empty spot:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15]  [20][60] [80,90,100]
30 is deleted. The tree remains balanced and all leaves are still at the same depth. ✓

Delete 50
50 is the root. Its inorder successor is 60 (smallest key in its right subtree). Swap 50 and 60:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15]  [20][50] [80,90,100]
Now delete 50 from the leaf [50]. It is a 2-node with no siblings to borrow from (both [20] and [60] in the right subtree are also 2-nodes).
In this case, we merge: combine the 2-node [50] with its sibling [60] (oops — actually [60] is now the root, not a sibling). Let’s be precise: the right child of the root is [70], whose left child is [50] and right child is [80,90,100]. Since [50] is a 2-node and we must delete from it, we can borrow from the rich sibling [80, 90, 100]. The sibling’s smallest key (80) rotates up to the parent [70], and 70 rotates down to fill the gap:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [80]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15] [20][70] [90,100]
50 is deleted. Final tree:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [80]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15] [20][70] [90,100]
Still height 2, all leaves at the same depth. ✓

📌 Key takeaway from deletion: The 2-3-4 tree never lets a node go empty. If you need to delete from a 2-node, you always first fatten it up — either by borrowing from a sibling or by merging with a sibling — before removing the key. This is the structural guarantee that keeps the tree balanced after every operation.

title: Indexing and Hashing
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages of 2-3-4 Trees
Advantages: - \(O(\log n)\) height — all operations guaranteed efficient. - All leaves at the same depth — no degenerate cases. - Sorted order maintained automatically. - Generalizes easily to larger nodes (B-trees). - Suitable as a foundation for external data structures (disk-based storage).
Disadvantage: - Multiple node types (2-node, 3-node, 4-node) — implementation requires constructing and destructing different node sizes during splits and merges, which is messy in practice.

💡 The connection to B-trees: If you use a single uniform node type with space for 3 keys and 4 pointers (and allow it to be partially filled), you get a B-tree. A 2-3-4 tree is exactly a B-tree with parameter \(n = 4\). B-trees (and their variant, B+-trees) are what real database engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL actually use for their indexes.

Index Definition in SQL
-- Create a basic index
CREATE INDEX emp_ename ON emp_tab(ename);

-- Create a unique index (enforces candidate key constraint)
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX emp_email ON emp_tab(email);

-- Create a composite index on two columns
CREATE INDEX emp_comp ON emp_tab(ename, empno) COMPUTE STATISTICS;

-- Function-based index (precomputes the function result for each row)
CREATE INDEX emp_upper ON emp_tab(UPPER(ename)) COMPUTE STATISTICS;

-- Bitmap index (best for columns with few distinct values)
CREATE BITMAP INDEX idx_gender ON student(gender);

-- Drop an index
DROP INDEX emp_ename;

💡 COMPUTE STATISTICS tells the optimizer to gather column statistics at index creation time — important for the optimizer to make good decisions.


📌 CREATE UNIQUE INDEX is technically redundant if you’ve already declared the column as UNIQUE in the table definition — the constraint is preferred.


Composite Indexes and Column Order
A composite index sorts entries lexicographically — first column first. An index on (dept_name, salary):

✓ Works for WHERE dept_name = 'Finance' AND salary = 80000
✓ Works for WHERE dept_name = 'Finance' AND salary < 80000
✗ Cannot efficiently handle WHERE dept_name < 'Finance' AND salary = 80000

The first column is the “anchor” — put the most selective column (most distinct values) first.

Multiple-Key Access
When a query filters on two columns, you have three strategies using single-attribute indexes:
SELECT ID FROM instructor
WHERE dept_name = 'Finance' AND salary = 80000;

Use the dept_name index → fetch all Finance instructors → filter by salary.
Use the salary index → fetch all at 80000 → filter by dept.
Use both indexes → take the intersection of the two pointer sets.

All three are less efficient than a single composite index on (dept_name, salary), which fetches only the exact records that satisfy both conditions.

text:
Guidelines for Indexing
Normalization is a one-time design decision. Indexing is ongoing — query patterns change, tables grow, and indexes that once helped may eventually hurt. The approach is to collect statistics, monitor performance, and adjust.
There are seven practical ground rules:

Rule 0 — Indexes Lead to an Access–Update Trade-off
Every index speeds up reads but adds overhead to every write. Unnecessary indexes also consume disk space and slow memory operations.

⚠️ Index deliberately. An index no query uses is pure overhead.



Rule 1 — Index the Correct Tables
Create an index when queries frequently retrieve less than ~15% of rows from a large table. Below that threshold, index lookup beats a full scan; above it, a full scan is often faster.
Also index: - Columns used in join conditions. - Foreign keys (primary/unique keys get indexes automatically; foreign keys usually don’t).

📌 Small tables don’t need indexes. If a query on a small table is suddenly slow, the table has probably grown large.



Rule 2 — Index the Correct Columns
Good candidates:







Column characteristic
Best index type




Many distinct values, wide range
Regular (B-tree) index


Few distinct values
Bitmap index


Many NULLs, but queries filter non-NULLs
Index + rewrite IS NOT NULL as a range predicate



Poor candidates: columns with many NULLs where queries don’t filter on non-NULL values; LONG/LONG RAW columns (cannot be indexed).


Rule 3 — Limit the Number of Indexes per Table
Every index on a table is updated on every INSERT, DELETE, or column UPDATE. The right count depends on the table’s workload:

Read-heavy (reports, lookups) → more indexes are fine.
Write-heavy (transactions, event logs) → fewer indexes, lower write overhead.



Rule 4 — Choose Column Order in Composite Indexes Carefully
Put the most selective column first. A composite index on (part_no, vendor_id) where there are 1000 part numbers but only 5 vendors:
CREATE INDEX idx ON vendor_parts(part_no, vendor_id);

✓ Helps queries on part_no alone (leading column).
✗ A standalone index on vendor_id alone would be useless — only 5 values.



Rule 5 — Gather Statistics
The query optimizer uses statistics (row counts, value distributions) to decide whether to use an index. Stale stats → bad decisions.
-- At creation time
CREATE INDEX idx ON emp_tab(ename) COMPUTE STATISTICS;

-- Periodic refresh (Oracle)
DBMS_STATS.GATHER_TABLE_STATISTICS(...);
DBMS_STATS.GATHER_SCHEMA_STATISTICS(...);


Rule 6 — Drop Indexes That Are No Longer Required
Drop an index if: - It doesn’t speed up any current query. - The application no longer issues queries that use it. - You need to rebuild it (must drop first).
DROP INDEX emp_ename;
Dropping an index returns its storage to the tablespace immediately.

Indexing
text:
Multiple-Key Access
When a query filters on two columns, you have three strategies using single-attribute indexes:
SELECT ID FROM instructor
WHERE dept_name = 'Finance' AND salary = 80000;

Use the dept_name index → fetch all Finance instructors → filter by salary.
Use the salary index → fetch all at 80000 → filter by dept.
Use both indexes → take the intersection of the two pointer sets.

All three are less efficient than a single composite index on (dept_name, salary), which fetches only the exact records that satisfy both conditions.

title: Indexing
text:
Guidelines for Indexing
Indexing is an ongoing task — query patterns change, tables grow, and indexes need to be monitored and adjusted over time.

Rule 1: Index the Correct Tables
Rule 2: Index the Correct Columns
Rule 3: Limit the Number of Indexes for Each Table
Rule 4: Choose the Order of Columns in Composite Indexes
Rule 5: Gather Statistics to Make Index Usage More Accurate
Rule 6: Drop Indexes That Are No Longer Required

text:
Quick Reference: The Seven Rules








Rule
Name
Core idea




0

Indexes speed reads, slow writes — index deliberately


1
Index the Correct Tables

2

Fewer on write-heavy tables; more on read-heavy

Formulas for Solving the Problem
