title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Why Trees for Indexing?
The multilevel index from Section 1 was a good idea, but it had one major problem: as the file grows, overflow blocks pile up and performance degrades. You eventually need to reorganize the whole file — expensive and disruptive.
Tree-based structures solve this by self-balancing on every insert and delete, keeping search cost at \(O(\log n)\) always, without any manual reorganization.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Binary Search Trees (BST)
Searching \(n\) data items:



Method
Time
Structure




Linear Search
\(O(n)\)
Unordered array or list


Binary Search
\(O(\log n)\)
Sorted array


BST Search
\(O(h)\)
Tree, where \(h\) = height



For a BST with \(n\) nodes: \(\log n \leq h < n\).
The problem: \(h\) depends on insertion order.
Sorted insertion: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
Result:
  1
   \
    2
     \
      3   ← degenerate linked list, O(n) search
A BST is only useful when \(h \sim O(\log n)\) — i.e., when it is balanced.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Balanced BSTs
A BST is balanced when \(h \sim O(\log n)\). Balancing can be guaranteed in different ways:








Type
Guarantee
How




AVL Tree
Worst-case
\(\|h_L - h_R\| \leq 1\) at every node; rotations on violation


Randomized BST
Expected
Keys inserted in random order — root has equal probability \(\frac{1}{n}\)


Skip List
Probabilistic
Layered linked lists built probabilistically


Splay Tree
Amortized
Recently accessed nodes moved to root



All achieve \(O(\log n)\) for search, insert, and delete.
But they all share a critical limitation:

⚠️ Balanced BSTs work well in memory but do not scale to disk. Each node access = one disk read (~20ms). With \(O(\log n)\) levels, searching 1 million records in a BST needs ~20 disk reads. That’s too slow.

The fix: make nodes fatter — store multiple keys per node, fewer levels, fewer disk reads.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
The 2-3-4 Tree: Motivation
The problem with BSTs on disk is that each node holds only one key and has only two children. The tree must be very tall (\(O(\log n)\) levels) to hold \(n\) records.
What if we could make each node fatter — storing multiple keys and having multiple children? Then the tree would be much shorter, and we’d need far fewer disk reads to reach any record. This idea leads to the 2-3-4 Tree.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
What Is a 2-3-4 Tree?
A 2-3-4 Tree is a balanced search tree where every node can hold 1, 2, or 3 keys (and correspondingly have 2, 3, or 4 children). That is where the name comes from.
The three node types:









Node type
Keys stored
Children
Search key rule




2-node
1 (call it S)
2
left child < S; right child > S


3-node
2 (S and L)
3
left < S; middle: S–L; right > L


4-node
3 (S, M, L)
4
left < S; second: S–M; third: M–L; right > L



A leaf node can hold 1, 2, or 3 data items.
Key properties:

All leaves sit at the same depth — the tree is always perfectly height-balanced.
\(h \sim O(\log n)\), so search, insert, and delete all cost \(O(\log n)\).
Data is always kept in sorted order.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Search in a 2-3-4 Tree
Search is a straightforward extension of BST search. At each node, compare the target key against the node’s keys and follow the appropriate child pointer. Repeat until you reach a leaf or find the key.

💡 Because all leaves are at the same depth, every search takes exactly \(O(h) = O(\log n)\) steps — no worst-case skew possible.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Insertion in a 2-3-4 Tree
Insertion always happens at a leaf. The process:

Search for the expected location (the leaf where the key would go).
If the leaf is a 2-node, expand it to a 3-node and insert. Done.
If the leaf is a 3-node, expand it to a 4-node and insert. Done.
If the leaf is a 4-node, we can’t add another key — we must split it first.


Node Splitting
Splitting a 4-node takes its middle key (M) and pushes it up to the parent. The original 4-node becomes two 2-nodes (one holding S, one holding L), both children of the parent which now absorbs M.
There are three cases depending on the parent:
Case 1 — Parent is the root (a 4-node):
    [S  M  L]          [M]
   /  |  |  \    →    /   \
  a   b  c   d      [S]   [L]
                   / \   / \
                  a   b c   d
The tree grows one level taller.
Case 2 — Parent is a 2-node:
The middle key M is absorbed into the parent, converting it from a 2-node to a 3-node. The split 4-node’s two halves (S and L) become two separate children.
Case 3 — Parent is a 3-node:
Same idea — M is absorbed, converting the parent from a 3-node to a 4-node.


Early vs. Late Splitting
There are two strategies for when to split:

Early splitting: Split any 4-node you encounter on the way down during a search, before you actually need to. This ensures you never have a full node at the insertion point. At most one split per level.
Late splitting: Only split when you actually need to insert into a 4-node. May cascade up \(O(h)\) splits in the worst case.

Both strategies produce valid trees with the same complexity \(O(h)\), but they produce different final shapes. The slides follow the early splitting strategy.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Insertion Example: Step by Step
Inserting the sequence 10, 30, 60, 20, 50, 40, 70, 80, 15, 90, 100 using the early splitting strategy.

After inserting 10, 30, 60 — all three fit into one leaf (a 4-node):
[10  30  60]

Insert 20 — the root is a 4-node, so we split it before descending. Middle key 30 becomes the new root; 10 and 60 become separate children. Then 20 is inserted into the left child:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [60]

Insert 50 — 50 > 30, go right. [60] is a 2-node, so just expand it:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [50, 60]

Insert 40 — 40 > 30, go right. [50, 60] is a 3-node, expand to 4-node and insert:
        [30]
       /    \
  [10, 20]  [40, 50, 60]

Insert 70 — root [30] is fine. 70 > 30, descend right. [40, 50, 60] is a 4-node — split it immediately (early strategy). Middle key 50 rises to join the root:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60]
Now insert 70 into the right child [60]:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60, 70]

Insert 80 — 80 > 50, go to right child [60, 70]. It’s a 3-node, expand it:
           [30, 50]
          /   |    \
   [10,20]  [40]  [60, 70, 80]

Insert 15 — 15 < 30, go left. [10, 20] is a 3-node, expand it:
              [30, 50]
             /   |    \
  [10, 15, 20]  [40]  [60, 70, 80]

Insert 90 — root [30, 50] is fine. 90 > 50, descend right. [60, 70, 80] is a 4-node — split it. Middle key 70 rises to join the root:
                [30, 50, 70]
               /   |    |   \
  [10,15,20]  [40] [60] [80]
Now insert 90 into the rightmost child [80]:
                [30, 50, 70]
               /   |    |   \
  [10,15,20]  [40] [60] [80, 90]

Insert 100 — root [30, 50, 70] is a 4-node — split it first. Middle key 50 becomes the new root; 30 and 70 become children:
                      [50]
                     /    \
                  [30]    [70]
                 /    \   /   \
          [10,15,20] [40] [60] [80,90]
Now insert 100. 100 > 50 → go right to [70]. 100 > 70 → go to right child [80, 90]. It’s a 3-node, expand it:
                      [50]
                     /    \
                  [30]    [70]
                 /    \   /   \
          [10,15,20] [40] [60] [80, 90, 100]

Final tree after all 11 insertions:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [30]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [40][60] [80,90,100]
Height = 2. All 11 keys stored, all leaves at the same level.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Deletion in a 2-3-4 Tree
Deletion is the reverse of insertion. The core idea:

Locate the node containing the target key.
Swap it with its inorder successor (the smallest key in the right subtree). This reduces deletion to always happening at a leaf.
If the leaf is a 3-node or 4-node, simply remove the key.
If the leaf is a 2-node, removing its only key would leave an empty node — which is illegal. To prevent this, transform every 2-node you encounter (on the way down) into a 3-node or 4-node first. This is the reverse of the splitting cases from insertion.


Deletion Example
We will delete 30 and then 50 from the final tree above.
Starting tree:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [30]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [40][60] [80,90,100]

Delete 30
30 is an internal node. Its inorder successor is 40 (smallest key in its right subtree). Swap 30 and 40:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [40]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15,20] [30][60] [80,90,100]
Now delete 30 from the leaf [30]. That leaf is a 2-node — but since 30 is the only key, removing it would leave an empty node.
However, looking at its sibling [10, 15, 20] (a 4-node), we can borrow from it. The sibling’s largest key (20) rotates up to the parent, and the parent’s key (40) rotates down to fill the now-empty spot:
                         [50]
                        /    \
                     [20]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15]  [40][60] [80,90,100]
30 is deleted. The tree remains balanced and all leaves are still at the same depth.

Delete 50
50 is the root. Its inorder successor is 60 (smallest key in its right subtree). Swap 50 and 60:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [20]    [70]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15]    [40][50] [80,90,100]
Now delete 50 from the leaf [50]. It is a 2-node with no siblings to borrow from (both [20] and [60] in the right subtree are also 2-nodes).
In this case, we merge: combine the 2-node [50] with its sibling [60] (oops — actually [60] is now the root, not a sibling). Let’s be precise: the right child of the root is [70], whose left child is [50] and right child is [80,90,100]. Since [50] is a 2-node and we must delete from it, we can borrow from the rich sibling [80, 90, 100]. The sibling’s smallest key (80) rotates up to the parent [70], and 70 rotates down to fill the gap:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [20]    [80]
                    /    \   /   \
             [10,15]    [40][70] [90,100]
50 is deleted. Final tree:
                         [60]
                        /    \
                     [20]    [80]
                    /    \   /   \
               [10,15]  [40][70] [90,100]
Still height 2, all leaves at the same depth.

📌 Key takeaway from deletion: The 2-3-4 tree never lets a node go empty. If you need to delete from a 2-node, you always first fatten it up — either by borrowing from a sibling or by merging with a sibling — before removing the key. This is the structural guarantee that keeps the tree balanced after every operation.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Advantages and Disadvantages of 2-3-4 Trees
Advantages: - \(O(\log n)\) height — all operations guaranteed efficient. - All leaves at the same depth — no degenerate cases. - Sorted order maintained automatically. - Generalizes easily to larger nodes (B-trees). - Suitable as a foundation for external data structures (disk-based storage).
Disadvantage: - Multiple node types (2-node, 3-node, 4-node) — implementation requires constructing and destructing different node sizes during splits and merges, which is messy in practice.

💡 The connection to B-trees: If you use a single uniform node type with space for 3 keys and 4 pointers (and allow it to be partially filled), you get a B-tree. A 2-3-4 tree is exactly a B-tree with parameter \(n = 4\). B-trees (and their variant, B+-trees) are what real database engines like PostgreSQL and MySQL actually use for their indexes.

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Putting It All Together







Concept
What it solves




Ordered index
Enables fast lookup without scanning the whole table


Dense vs. sparse
Trade-off between index size and lookup speed


Primary vs. secondary
One physical order → one primary; unlimited secondaries


Multilevel index
Handles indexes too large to fit in memory


BST (balanced)
Optimal in-memory search: \(O(\log n)\)


2-3-4 tree
Extends balanced search to external storage; precursor to B-trees



The progression is logical: plain indexing → layered indexing → tree-structured indexing → multi-key node trees → B/B+-trees (next topic).

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
The B+ Tree
The B+ tree is what databases actually use. It fixes the ISAM problem — no overflow blocks, no full-file reorganization, self-balancing on every change.
Why B+ over balanced BST?
With \(n = 100\) keys per node and 1 million records: B+ tree needs 4 disk reads vs ~20 for a balanced BST. Each read costs ~20ms — that difference matters at scale.


Structure
A B+ tree with parameter \(n\) satisfies:







Node
Children / Values




Internal node (non-root)
Between \(\lceil n/2 \rceil\) and \(n\) children


Root (non-leaf)
At least 2 children


Leaf node
Between \(\lceil (n-1)/2 \rceil\) and \(n-1\) values


Root as leaf
Between 0 and \(n-1\) values



All paths from root to leaf are the same length.
Key distinction from 2-3-4 tree: leaf nodes are linked together in a linked list, enabling efficient sequential (range) access in addition to random access.



Node Layout
Each node holds keys \(K_1 < K_2 < \cdots < K_{n-1}\) and pointers \(P_1, P_2, \ldots, P_n\).
Leaf node: \(P_i\) points to the actual data record with key \(K_i\). The last pointer \(P_n\) points to the next leaf in sorted order.
Internal node: \(P_i\) points to a subtree. Routing rule: - Keys in subtree \(P_1\) are \(< K_1\) - Keys in subtree \(P_i\) (\(2 \leq i \leq n-1\)) are \(\geq K_{i-1}\) and \(< K_i\) - Keys in subtree \(P_n\) are \(\geq K_{n-1}\)

📌 Example (n = 6): Leaf nodes hold 3–5 values. Internal nodes hold 3–6 children. Root has at least 2 children.




Search
To find value \(V\):

Start at root \(C\).
While \(C\) is not a leaf: find the least \(i\) such that \(V \leq K_i\). If none exists, follow the last pointer. Otherwise follow \(P_{i+1}\) if \(V = K_i\), else \(P_i\).
At leaf \(C\): find least \(i\) such that \(K_i = V\). If found, follow \(P_i\) to the record. If not, the record doesn’t exist.

Height bound: at most \(\lceil \log_{\lceil n/2 \rceil}(K) \rceil\) levels for \(K\) search-key values.



Handling Duplicate Keys
With duplicates, the strict \(K_1 < K_2 < \cdots\) ordering becomes \(K_1 \leq K_2 \leq \cdots\).
Modified search: when \(V = K_i\) at an internal node, still descend into \(P_i\) (not \(P_{i+1}\)), since a duplicate of \(V\) may exist in the left subtree. At the leaf, if all values are \(< V\), move to the right sibling before checking.
To find all occurrences: find the first occurrence, then traverse consecutive leaf nodes via the linked list.



Insertion

Find the leaf where the key belongs.
If space exists: insert the (key, pointer) pair in sorted order. Done.
If leaf is full: split the leaf.


Splitting a Leaf Node

Take all \(n\) (key, pointer) pairs including the new one, sorted.
Put the first \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor\) in the original node, the rest in a new node.
Let \(k\) = smallest key in the new node. Insert \((k, \text{new node pointer})\) into the parent.
If the parent is also full, split it — propagate upward.



Splitting an Internal Node

Copy the full node + new entry into a temporary buffer of \(n+1\) pointers and \(n\) keys.
Keep \(P_1, K_1, \ldots, K_{\lceil n/2 \rceil - 1}, P_{\lceil n/2 \rceil}\) in the original node.
Put \(P_{\lceil n/2 \rceil + 1}, K_{\lceil n/2 \rceil + 1}, \ldots\) in a new node.
Push \(K_{\lceil n/2 \rceil}\) up to the parent.

Splits propagate upward until a non-full node is found. In the worst case, the root splits and the tree grows one level taller.




Deletion

Find and remove the record from the file (and its bucket if applicable).
Remove the (key, pointer) from the leaf.
If the node still has enough entries: done.
If underfull and can merge with sibling: combine both nodes into one; delete the separator key from the parent (recursively).
If underfull but cannot merge: redistribute — borrow from a sibling and update the separator key in the parent.

Deletions can cascade upward. If the root ends up with only one child after a deletion, delete the root and promote its sole child as the new root.



B+ Tree File Organization
Standard B+ trees store pointers to records in leaf nodes. B+ tree file organization stores the actual records in leaf nodes instead.

Solves data file degradation (not just index degradation).
Leaf nodes must still be at least half full.
Since records are larger than pointers, fewer entries fit per leaf than in an index B+ tree.
Insertions and deletions work identically.


💡 To improve space utilization, involve two siblings in redistribution during splits/merges. This guarantees each node has at least \(\lfloor 2n/3 \rfloor\) entries.




Non-Unique Search Keys
Three approaches when the same key value appears in multiple records:








Approach
Overhead
Notes




Separate bucket blocks
High space/IO
Generally a bad idea


List of tuple pointers per key
Low space
Deletion is expensive with many duplicates


Append record-id to key
Small storage overhead
Simplest code; most widely used



The record-id approach makes every key unique artificially, so standard insert/delete logic applies without modification.



Record Relocation and Secondary Indices
When a record moves (e.g., due to a node split in B+ tree file organization), every secondary index storing a direct record pointer must be updated — expensive.
Solution: store the primary index search key in the secondary index instead of a direct record pointer.

Lookup: secondary index → primary key → primary index → record (one extra traversal).
Node splits only require updating the primary index; secondary indices are untouched.
If the primary key is non-unique, append the record-id.




Indexing Strings
Variable-length string keys introduce variable fanout — nodes can hold different numbers of keys depending on key lengths. Space utilization becomes the split criterion instead of a fixed pointer count.
Prefix compression reduces this problem: - Internal nodes only need enough of a key to distinguish between subtrees. “Silas” and “Silberschatz” can be separated by just “Silb”. - Leaf nodes can compress keys by sharing common prefixes.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
What is Hashing?
Instead of searching through a sorted structure, hashing computes exactly which bucket a record lives in — no traversal needed. Think of it as a direct address calculator.
A hash function \(h\) maps a search key to a bucket address:
\[h : \text{search-key values} \rightarrow \text{bucket addresses}\]
A good hash function is uniform (distributes keys evenly across all buckets) and fast to compute.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
A bucket is a unit of storage — typically one disk block — holding one or more records.
If \(h(k_1) = h(k_2)\) for \(k_1 \neq k_2\), a collision has occurred.



⚠️ The worst hash function maps every key to the same bucket — search degrades to \(O(n)\).

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Static Hashing
The number of buckets \(B\) is fixed at creation time.
Lookup: compute \(h(k)\) → go directly to that bucket → scan within it sequentially.
Example: 10 buckets, keys are department names. Hash = sum of character values mod 10.
h(Music)      = 1    h(History)   = 2
h(Physics)    = 3    h(Elec. Eng.) = 3   ← collision
Physics and Elec. Eng. both map to bucket 3. Both records are stored there and the bucket is scanned sequentially to find the right one.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Handling Bucket Overflow
Overflow happens when a bucket fills up. Causes:

Too few buckets allocated initially.
Skew — many records share the same key, or the hash function distributes unevenly.

Solution: overflow chaining — link overflow buckets to the original in a linked list.
Bucket 3: [Physics | Elec. Eng.] → [overflow block] → ...
This scheme is called closed hashing.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Hash Indices
Hashing can also be used purely as an index structure (not file organization). A hash index organizes search keys and their record pointers into a hash structure.

Strictly speaking, hash indices are always secondary indices — if the file is already hash-organized on the same key, a separate hash index is redundant.
Used like other secondary indices: compute \(h(k)\), find the bucket, scan for the pointer, follow it to the record.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Deficiencies of Static Hashing
The fixed bucket count \(B\) is the core problem:







Scenario
Problem




File grows beyond initial estimate
Too many overflow chains → poor performance


File shrinks
Mostly empty buckets → wasted space


\(B\) set too large from the start
Space wasted immediately



Periodic full reorganization with a new hash function is possible but expensive and disruptive.
Better fix: let the number of buckets grow and shrink dynamically.

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Dynamic Hashing (Extendable Hashing)
Instead of a fixed bucket count, extendable hashing uses a directory (bucket address table) that doubles or halves as needed.

Core Idea

The hash function produces a \(b\)-bit integer (typically \(b = 32\)).
Only the first \(i\) bits (global depth) are used to index into the directory.
Directory size = \(2^i\). Initially \(i = 0\).
Each bucket \(j\) stores its own local depth \(i_j\) — how many bits actually identify its entries.
Multiple directory entries can point to the same bucket when \(i_j < i\).




Dynamic Hashing





Lookup

Compute \(h(k) = X\).
Use the first \(i\) bits of \(X\) as a directory index.
Follow the pointer to the bucket and scan within it.




Insertion

Lookup the target bucket \(j\).
If space exists → insert. Done.
If bucket \(j\) is full → split:

Case 1 — \(i > i_j\) (multiple entries point to \(j\)): - Allocate new bucket \(z\), set \(i_j = i_z = i_j + 1\). - Redirect the second half of entries that pointed to \(j\) → now point to \(z\). - Redistribute all records in \(j\) between \(j\) and \(z\) by recomputing hash prefixes. - Retry insertion.
Case 2 — \(i = i_j\) (only one entry points to \(j\)): - Increment \(i\), double the directory (each old entry becomes two entries pointing to the same bucket). - Now \(i > i_j\) → apply Case 1. - If \(i\) hits limit \(b\) or too many splits occur, use an overflow bucket instead.



Deletion

Remove the record from its bucket.
If the bucket empties, it can be removed.
Coalesce with a “buddy” bucket — a bucket with the same \(i_j\) and the same \((i_j - 1)\)-bit prefix.
Shrink the directory if the actual bucket count becomes much smaller than \(2^i\) (expensive — do sparingly).




Extendable Hashing: Pros and Cons







✓ Advantages
✗ Disadvantages




Performance doesn’t degrade as file grows
Extra level of indirection on every lookup


Minimal space overhead
Directory can exceed memory size


No periodic reorganization needed
Doubling the directory is expensive




💡 If the directory outgrows memory, a B+ tree can index into it — combining the benefits of both structures.

text:
Ordered Indexing vs. Hashing



Factor
B+ Tree (Ordered)
Hash Index




Point lookup
\(O(\log n)\)
\(O(1)\) average


Range queries
✓ Efficient
✗ Not supported


Worst-case access
Guaranteed \(O(\log n)\)
Degrades with overflow


Reorganization
Never needed
Needed for static hashing



Rule of thumb: use hashing for exact-match lookups; use ordered indices when range queries are common.
In practice:



System
Hash support




PostgreSQL
Supports hash indices but discourages them


Oracle
Supports static hash file organization; no hash indices


SQL Server
B+ trees only

title: Hashing and Bitmap Indices
text:
Bitmap Indices
Bitmap indices are designed for multi-attribute analytical queries on low-cardinality columns — not for point lookups.

What They Are
For an attribute with \(m\) distinct values, a bitmap index stores \(m\) bit vectors — one per distinct value. Each bit vector has one bit per record:

1 if the record has that value.
0 otherwise.

Example: gender attribute, 5 records:
Record:     0  1  2  3  4

title: Tree-Based Index Structures
text:
Search
To find value \(V\):

Start at root \(C\).
While \(C\) is not a leaf: find least \(i\) such that \(V \leq K_i\). Follow \(P_{i+1}\) if \(V = K_i\), else \(P_i\). If no such \(i\), follow last pointer.
At leaf: if \(K_i = V\), follow \(P_i\) to record. Else record doesn’t exist.

Duplicates: ordering relaxes to \(\leq\). Always descend \(P_i\) when \(V = K_i\) — duplicates may exist in the left subtree. To find all occurrences, traverse consecutive leaves via the linked list.

Insertion

Find the target leaf and insert in sorted order.
If space exists → insert. Done.
If leaf is full → split:

Put first \(\lfloor n/2 \rfloor\) pairs in original node, rest in new node.
Push smallest key of new node up to parent.

If parent is also full → split it and propagate upward.
Worst case: root splits, tree grows one level taller.

Remove the record and its (key, pointer) from the leaf.
Node still has enough entries → done.
Underfull + can merge with sibling → combine into one node; pull separator key down from parent; recurse upward.
Underfull + cannot merge → redistribute from sibling; update separator key in parent.
If root ends up with one child → delete root, promote that child.

Record relocation: if a record moves, every secondary index storing a direct pointer must be updated. Fix: store the primary search key in the secondary index instead — one extra traversal on lookup, but node splits are cheap.

title: (Optional) Real-World Concurrency
text:
Theory vs. Practice
Throughout this week, we’ve explored strict theoretical protocols like Two-Phase Locking (2PL) and Timestamp-based protocols. However, if you spin up a real, modern database like PostgreSQL or MySQL (InnoDB), you’ll find that they don’t strictly use standard 2PL for everything.
Why? Because standard 2PL forces reads to block writes, and writes to block reads. In a massive web application with thousands of concurrent users, this level of locking would cause unacceptable performance bottlenecks.
Modern databases solve this using a hybrid approach called MVCC.

title: (Optional) Real-World Concurrency
text:
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC)
MVCC is the secret sauce behind almost all modern enterprise relational databases.
The core philosophy of MVCC is simple: “Readers do not block Writers, and Writers do not block Readers.”

How does it work?
Instead of locking a row when it’s being updated, the database simply creates a new version of that row.

Transaction A wants to update a row (e.g., change Alice’s balance from $100 to $50). It writes a brand new version of the row to the disk but doesn’t delete the old one yet.
Transaction B comes along and wants to read Alice’s balance.
Because Transaction A hasn’t committed yet, Transaction B ignores the new version and reads the old version ($100). No locks required!
Once Transaction A commits, any future transactions will see the new version ($50).

Under the hood, this uses the Timestamp Protocols we learned about! Every transaction gets an ID (a timestamp), and every row version is tagged with the transaction IDs that created and deleted it. The database uses these tags to mathematically determine which version of a row a specific transaction is allowed to “see”.

title: (Optional) Real-World Concurrency
text:
Isolation Levels in Practice
Because perfect serializability is expensive, SQL standards allow developers to choose their desired Isolation Level for a transaction. This allows you to trade safety for speed depending on your specific use case.
From most dangerous (fastest) to safest (slowest):

Read Uncommitted: A transaction can read uncommitted “dirty” data from other transactions. (Extremely fast, but very dangerous).
Read Committed: (Default in PostgreSQL) A transaction can only read data that has been fully committed. However, if it reads the same row twice, the value might change if another transaction committed an update in between.
Repeatable Read: (Default in MySQL) Guarantees that if you read a row twice in the same transaction, you will see the exact same data both times, even if another transaction updated it.
Serializable: The absolute strictest level. The database guarantees the result is mathematically identical to serial execution. If it detects a conflict that breaks serializability, it simply aborts one of the transactions.


The Trade-off
Most companies do not run their databases in Serializable mode because the performance penalty and frequency of deadlocks/aborts is too high. They run in Read Committed or Repeatable Read, accepting minor theoretical inconsistencies in exchange for massive concurrency gains.

title: Transactions and ACID Properties
text:
Introduction to Transactions
When you use a database, you don’t typically run just a single isolated query. Often, you need to run a sequence of queries to accomplish a logical task.
A Transaction is a unit of program execution that accesses and, possibly, updates various data items. It represents a single logical unit of work.

title: Transactions and ACID Properties
text:
The Big Challenges
When managing transactions, databases have to overcome two massive hurdles:

System Failures: What happens if the hardware crashes right in the middle of a transaction?
Concurrent Execution: What happens if two different transactions try to update the exact same row of data at the exact same millisecond?

title: Transactions and ACID Properties
text:
The ACID Properties
To solve these challenges and guarantee database reliability, every transaction must adhere to four strict rules, famously known by the acronym ACID.

1. Atomicity (All or Nothing)
A transaction is treated as a single, indivisible unit. Either all of its instructions execute successfully, or none of them do. There is no such thing as a partially completed transaction.


2. Consistency
Execution of a transaction in isolation preserves the consistency of the database. If the database was in a valid state before the transaction, it must be in a valid state after the transaction completes.


3. Isolation
Even though transactions may be executing concurrently, the system guarantees that each transaction is unaware of the others. The end result must be equivalent to if the transactions had run sequentially, one after the other.


4. Durability
Once a transaction has committed successfully, its changes to the database are permanent, even if the system crashes immediately afterward.

title: Transactions and ACID Properties
text:
A Classic Example: Bank Transfer
Let’s look at the textbook example of transferring $50 from Account A to Account B. This is a single logical transaction, but it consists of several steps.



Step
Instruction
Meaning




1
read(A)
Get the current balance of Account A.


2
A := A - 50
Deduct $50 from A’s balance.


3
write(A)
Save the new balance of A to the database.


4
read(B)
Get the current balance of Account B.


5
B := B + 50
Add $50 to B’s balance.


6
write(B)
Save the new balance of B to the database.



Let’s evaluate this against our ACID properties:

Atomicity: Imagine the system crashes precisely after Step 3. Account A has lost $50, but Account B hasn’t received it! The $50 just vanished. Atomicity ensures that if it fails here, the database will automatically roll back the changes to Account A, as if the transaction never started.
Consistency: The sum of A + B must remain exactly the same before and after the transaction.
Isolation: If another transaction tries to read Account A at Step 4, it might read the partially updated state. Isolation ensures this intermediate state is hidden.

title: Transactions and ACID Properties
text:
Transaction States
As a transaction progresses from start to finish, it passes through several defined states.



The lifecycle states of a transaction.



Active: The initial state. The transaction stays in this state while it is executing.
Partially Committed: After the final statement has been executed, but before the changes have been permanently recorded.
Committed: After successful completion. The changes are now durable and permanent.
Failed: Occurs when normal execution can no longer proceed (e.g., due to a software error, constraint violation, or hardware crash).
Aborted: After the transaction has been rolled back and the database has been restored to its prior state. From here, the transaction can either be restarted or killed entirely.

title: Schedules and Serializability
text:
What is a Schedule?
When multiple transactions are executed concurrently, their instructions are interleaved. A Schedule is simply a sequence of instructions that specifies the chronological order in which the instructions of concurrent transactions are executed.

title: Schedules and Serializability
text:
A schedule must consist of all instructions from the participating transactions.
It must preserve the order in which the instructions appeared in their original transactions.


Serial vs. Concurrent Schedules

Serial Schedule: Transactions run one after the other. Transaction A finishes completely before Transaction B begins. This guarantees database consistency, but it is extremely slow.
Concurrent Schedule: Instructions from multiple transactions are interleaved. This improves performance and resource utilization, but risks creating an inconsistent database state.




An example showing how an interleaved concurrent schedule can be equivalent to a serial schedule.

title: Schedules and Serializability
text:
Serializability
A concurrent schedule is considered Serializable if its final outcome is identical to that of some purely serial schedule. If we can prove a schedule is serializable, we guarantee it preserves database consistency!
There are two primary ways to determine this: Conflict Serializability and View Serializability.

1. Conflict Serializability
To understand conflict serializability, we first need to define what a “conflict” is.






NoteConflicting Instructions



Let \(I_i\) and \(I_j\) be two instructions from different transactions, operating on the exact same data item \(Q\) (e.g. a column in a table, like student_name).

\(read(Q)\) and \(read(Q)\) \(\rightarrow\) NO CONFLICT
\(read(Q)\) and \(write(Q)\) \(\rightarrow\) CONFLICT
\(write(Q)\) and \(read(Q)\) \(\rightarrow\) CONFLICT
\(write(Q)\) and \(write(Q)\) \(\rightarrow\) CONFLICT

If an instruction is just a read, they don’t conflict. If at least one instruction is a write, they conflict because the order in which they are executed changes the final value or the value read!


If a concurrent schedule can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting adjacent instructions, we say the schedule is Conflict Serializable.



Demonstrating how a schedule can be transformed into a serial schedule by swapping non-conflicting instructions.



The Precedence Graph
Checking every possible swap is tedious. Instead, we use a Precedence Graph:

Draw a node for each transaction.
Draw a directed edge from \(T_i\) to \(T_j\) if they have conflicting instructions and \(T_i\) executed first.







ImportantThe Acyclic Rule



A schedule is conflict serializable if and only if its precedence graph contains NO cycles (it is acyclic).





A transaction table and its corresponding Precedence Graph. Since there is a cycle (T1 -> T2 -> T1 is possible, though the image shows a complex graph), it would not be conflict serializable.


(Note: If the graph is acyclic, you can use topological sorting to find the exact serial execution order).



2. View Serializability
View serializability is a slightly looser definition than conflict serializability. Two schedules are “view equivalent” if they meet three conditions for every data item:

Initial Read: If \(T_i\) reads the initial value of \(Q\) in the first schedule, it must do so in the second.
Write-Read Pair: If \(T_j\) reads a value of \(Q\) written by \(T_i\) in the first schedule, it must read the value written by that exact same \(T_i\) in the second.
Final Write: The transaction that performs the last write to \(Q\) must be the same in both schedules.

Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable. However, some view-serializable schedules are not conflict-serializable. This usually happens when there are Blind Writes (writing to a variable without ever reading it first).

title: Schedules and Serializability
text:
Recovery and Cascading
If a transaction fails halfway through, we must roll it back to maintain the ACID property of Atomicity. This rollback process is known as Recovery. However, rolling back one transaction can cause a domino effect.

Recoverable Schedules
If Transaction B reads data written by Transaction A, then A must commit before B commits.



A non-recoverable schedule. If T8 aborts after T9 has already committed based on T8’s bad data, the database is ruined.




Cascading Rollbacks
Even if a schedule is recoverable, we can run into Cascading Rollbacks. If one transaction fails, every other transaction that read its dirty data must also be rolled back. This wastes a massive amount of computational work.



A cascading rollback. If T10 fails, T11 and T12 must also be rolled back.




Cascadeless Schedules
To prevent cascading rollbacks, databases enforce Cascadeless Schedules. Rule: Transaction B cannot even read data written by Transaction A until Transaction A has fully committed. (Note: Every cascadeless schedule is inherently recoverable).

title: Schedules and Serializability
Concurrency and Locking
text:
The Need for Concurrency Control
We know that a schedule must be both conflict serializable and recoverable (preferably cascadeless). However, allowing transactions to just run wildly and hoping the schedule turns out serializable is a terrible strategy.
The database needs a Concurrency Control mechanism to enforce these rules dynamically as transactions arrive.
There is always a trade-off: The more strict the concurrency control scheme, the safer the data is, but the slower the database runs (because transactions have to wait in line).

title: Concurrency and Locking
text: A bad concurrent schedule. Because T1 unlocked B too early without proper concurrency control, T2 read an inconsistent state!

title: Concurrency and Locking
text:
Lock-Based Protocols
The most common way to control concurrency is by using Locks. Think of a lock like a bathroom key. If someone has the key, nobody else can enter until they give it back.
Data items can be locked in two modes:

Exclusive (X) mode: The data item can be both read AND written.
Shared (S) mode: The data item can ONLY be read.


The Lock-Compatibility Matrix
Before a transaction can lock an item, it must request it from the lock manager. The lock manager checks the compatibility matrix:



State of the lock
Request: Shared
Request: Exclusive




Shared
Yes
No


Exclusive
No
No




Sharing is caring: Any number of transactions can hold Shared locks on the same item at the same time (since reading doesn’t change the data).
Exclusivity: If any transaction holds an Exclusive lock, no other transaction can hold any lock on that item. They must wait.

A transaction must hold a lock on a data item for as long as it is actively accessing it. Once it’s done, it releases it using the unlock(Q) instruction.

title: Concurrency and Locking
text:
The Two-Phase Locking Protocol (2PL)
Just having locks isn’t enough to guarantee serializability. If a transaction locks an item, modifies it, unlocks it, and then locks another item, we can still run into consistency issues.
To solve this, databases use the Two-Phase Locking (2PL) protocol. Under 2PL, every transaction goes through two distinct phases:

Growing Phase:

A transaction may obtain new locks.
It may not release any locks.

Shrinking Phase:

A transaction may release locks.
It may not obtain any new locks.


Once a transaction releases its very first lock, it has entered the Shrinking Phase and can never request another lock again.

Lock Conversions
During these phases, 2PL allows locks to be converted:

Growing Phase: You can upgrade a Shared lock to an Exclusive lock.
Shrinking Phase: You can downgrade an Exclusive lock to a Shared lock.

title: Concurrency and Locking
text:
Stricter Variants of 2PL
Standard 2PL guarantees serializability, but it does NOT guarantee cascadeless schedules. If a transaction fails during its Shrinking Phase after releasing some locks, other transactions might have already read its dirty data!
To prevent cascading rollbacks, databases use stricter versions of 2PL:

Strict Two-Phase Locking

Standard 2PL rules apply.
Addition: A transaction must hold all of its Exclusive locks until it fully commits or aborts.
Why? This guarantees that no other transaction can read its uncommitted changes.



Rigorous Two-Phase Locking

Standard 2PL rules apply.
Addition: A transaction must hold ALL of its locks (both Shared and Exclusive) until it commits or aborts.
Why? It is even safer and easier to implement, and transactions can be serialized in the exact order they commit.







WarningThe Trade-off



As we move from standard 2PL \(\rightarrow\) Strict 2PL \(\rightarrow\) Rigorous 2PL, the system becomes safer and simpler. However, Concurrency goes down. Because locks are held longer, other transactions are forced to wait longer, slowing down the overall system performance.

title: Deadlocks and Timestamps
text:
Understanding Deadlocks
Locking protocols solve the problem of inconsistency, but they introduce a new problem: Deadlock.
Imagine Transaction A holds a lock on item X and is waiting for a lock on item Y. Meanwhile, Transaction B holds a lock on item Y and is waiting for a lock on item X.
Neither transaction can ever proceed. They are stuck waiting for each other indefinitely.
When a deadlock occurs, the system has no choice but to intervene. It must roll back (abort) one of the transactions to break the cycle and release its locks so the other can proceed.

title: Deadlocks and Timestamps
text:
A classic deadlock scenario where two transactions are waiting for each other.




Starvation
A related issue is Starvation. This occurs when a badly designed concurrency control manager repeatedly forces a transaction to wait forever, even without a deadlock. For example, if Transaction A wants an Exclusive lock, but a continuous stream of new transactions keep requesting and getting Shared locks on that item, Transaction A will starve. Alternatively, a transaction might be repeatedly chosen as the “victim” to be rolled back during deadlocks, never getting a chance to finish.

title: Deadlocks and Timestamps
text:
Deadlock Prevention
Rather than letting deadlocks happen and fixing them later, databases can use schemes to prevent them from ever occurring. These schemes often use Transaction Timestamps.
A Timestamp is a unique identifier assigned by the database that represents the exact moment a transaction started. An older transaction has a smaller timestamp, while a younger transaction has a larger timestamp.

1. The Wait-Die Scheme (Non-Preemptive)
Rule: Older transactions wait for younger ones. Younger transactions die.
If Transaction A requests a lock held by Transaction B:

If A is older than B \(\rightarrow\) A is allowed to wait.
If A is younger than B \(\rightarrow\) A is killed (dies) and rolled back.



2. The Wound-Wait Scheme (Preemptive)
Rule: Younger transactions wait for older ones. Older transactions wound (kill) younger ones.
If Transaction A requests a lock held by Transaction B:

If A is older than B \(\rightarrow\) A forces B to be killed (wounds it). B is rolled back and restarted later.
If A is younger than B \(\rightarrow\) A is allowed to wait.

title: Deadlocks and Timestamps
text:
Deadlock Detection
If a database doesn’t use prevention schemes, it must periodically check for deadlocks using a Wait-For Graph.

Vertices (Nodes): Represent active transactions.
Edges: A directed edge from \(T_i\) to \(T_j\) means that \(T_i\) is waiting for \(T_j\) to release a lock.







ImportantThe Cycle Rule



The system is in a deadlock state if and only if the wait-for graph has a cycle.


If a cycle is detected, the database selects a “victim” transaction and rolls it back.

title: Deadlocks and Timestamps
text:
Timestamp-Based Protocols
What if we didn’t use locks at all? Another way to handle concurrency is by strictly enforcing execution based on timestamps.
Every data item Q in the database maintains two timestamps:

W-timestamp(Q): The largest timestamp of any transaction that successfully wrote to Q.
R-timestamp(Q): The largest timestamp of any transaction that successfully read Q.


Read and Write Rules
Suppose Transaction \(T_i\) wants to read(Q):

If \(TS(T_i) < W\text{-timestamp}(Q)\): This means a younger transaction has already overwritten the data! \(T_i\) is trying to read the past. The read is rejected, and \(T_i\) is rolled back.
If \(TS(T_i) \ge W\text{-timestamp}(Q)\): The read is allowed! We update \(R\text{-timestamp}(Q)\) if \(T_i\)’s timestamp is larger.

Suppose Transaction \(T_i\) wants to write(Q):

If \(TS(T_i) < R\text{-timestamp}(Q)\): A younger transaction has already read the data assuming \(T_i\)’s write never happened. The write is rejected, and \(T_i\) is rolled back.
If \(TS(T_i) < W\text{-timestamp}(Q)\): A younger transaction has already overwritten the data. The write is rejected, and \(T_i\) is rolled back.
Otherwise, the write is allowed, and \(W\text{-timestamp}(Q)\) is updated.



Correctness and Drawbacks

Pros: It guarantees serializability and inherently prevents deadlocks (because no transaction ever waits for a lock—they just execute or get rolled back).
Cons: It does NOT guarantee cascadeless or recoverable schedules, so transaction failures can cause significant cascading rollbacks.

title: Backup and Recovery
text:
What is Backup and Recovery?
Imagine your database crashes due to a power failure. Without a backup, everything is gone. A backup is a copy of your database — data files, control files, logs — that lets you restore the system when something goes wrong.
Recovery is the process of using that backup to bring the database back to its last consistent state.

title: Backup
text:
What is Backup and Recovery?
Backup — a copy of the database (data files, control files, logs) that can be used to restore the system after a failure.
Recovery — restoring the database to its last known consistent state using the backup and transaction logs.







Type
What it copies




Physical Backup
Actual files — data files, control files, redo logs


Logical Backup
Logical objects — tables, views, procedures, functions






Why Backup?







Reason
Explanation




Disaster Recovery
Hardware failures, malware, human error can cause data loss


Client-Side Changes
Developers may need to roll back to a previous database version


Auditing
Organizations may need a snapshot of past data (e.g. for lawsuits)


Downtime Prevention
Without backup, failures cause data loss → application downtime → business damage






Types of Data to Back Up

Business Data — client/employee records, business rules and events.
System Data — configuration files, log files, software dependencies, disk images.
Media Files — photos, videos, graphics. Typically the largest in size.




Backup Strategies

Full Backup
A complete copy of everything — tables, indexes, procedures, views.

Must be done at least once before any other strategy.
Used daily when: 24/7 availability is not required, data size is small, or admin availability is limited.




✓ Advantages
✗ Disadvantages




Single backup set — simple recovery
Slowest to perform


No dependency between backups

With multiple transactions running at once, they share one buffer and one log. To keep recovery safe, uncommitted writes must not be visible to other transactions — enforced using exclusive locks held until commit or abort (strict two-phase locking).
Recovery runs in two phases:

Phase 1 — Redo Phase
Scan the log forward from the last checkpoint:

< Ti, Xj, V1, V2 > → write V2 to Xj.
< Ti start > → add Ti to the undo-list.
< Ti commit > or < Ti abort > → remove Ti from the undo-list.



Phase 2 — Undo Phase
Scan the log backwards until the undo-list is empty:

< Ti, Xj, V1, V2 > for Ti in undo-list → write V1 to Xj; write CLR < Ti, Xj, V1 >.
< Ti start > for Ti in undo-list → write < Ti abort >; remove Ti from undo-list.

The Problem with Early Lock Release
In standard recovery, undoing a transaction means restoring the old physical value — simple, straightforward. But some operations, like B+ tree insertions, release their locks early to improve concurrency. Once a lock is released, another transaction can modify the same data.
If T1 inserts (V1, R1) into a B+ tree node and then releases its lock, T2 can come in and modify the same node. At this point, we can’t undo T1 by restoring the old value — that would wipe out T2’s work too. Instead, we must undo T1 by executing the inverse operation (a delete).
This is called logical undo.



Physical vs. Logical Undo









Physical Undo
Logical Undo




How it works
Restore the old value from the log
Execute the inverse operation


When it’s used
Normal cases — locks held throughout
Early lock release (e.g. B+ tree ops)


Example
Write back V1 to X
Delete the entry that was inserted




📌 Redo is always physical — even for operations that use logical undo. Logical redo is too complex because the disk state may not be operation-consistent at the time of recovery.

To support logical undo, the system logs operations differently — not just the data values, but also what inverse operation to run.
Three log records for each operation:







Record
Written when




< Ti, Oj, operation-begin >
Operation starts


< Ti, X, V1, V2 >
Each physical update during the operation (old + new value)


< Ti, Oj, operation-end, U >
Operation completes — U contains the logical undo info



Example: inserting (K5, RID7) into B+ tree I9: - operation-begin logged. - Physical updates to tree nodes logged as usual. - operation-end logged with U = “delete (K5, RID7) from I9”.

Situation
Undo method




Crash/rollback before operation completes
operation-end not found → use physical undo (old values)


Crash/rollback after operation completes
operation-end found → use logical undo (run U)

Scan the log backwards for transaction Ti:







What you find
What to do




< Ti, X, V1, V2 >
Physical undo — write V1 to X; log < Ti, X, V1 >


< Ti, Oj, operation-end, U >
Logical undo — execute U; log < Ti, Oj, operation-abort >; skip back to operation-begin


< Ti, Oj, operation-abort >
Skip all records back to operation-begin (already undone — avoid double rollback)


Redo-only record
Ignore


< Ti, start >
Stop scan; write < Ti, abort >

Same two-phase structure as before, with logical undo added to the undo phase.
Phase 1 — Redo Phase (scan forward from last checkpoint): - Physically redo all updates for all transactions — committed, aborted, or incomplete. - Build the undo-list: add Ti on < Ti start >; remove on < Ti commit > or < Ti abort >.
Phase 2 — Undo Phase (scan backwards): - For each Ti in undo-list, apply rollback with logical undo as described above. - When < Ti start > is found, write < Ti abort > and remove from undo-list. - Stop when undo-list is empty.

💡 The undo phase uses a single shared backwards scan for all transactions being undone simultaneously — efficient and correct.

Factor

Onsite = fast restore but vulnerable to physical disasters. Offsite/cloud = disaster-safe but slower to restore

title: Failure Classification & Log-Based Recovery
text:
What is RAID?
A single disk has two problems: it’s slow, and it can fail. RAID solves both by combining multiple disks into what looks like one — spreading data across them for speed and duplicating it for safety.
The core risk of using many disks: a 100-disk system with each disk having an MTTF of 100,000 hours ends up with a system MTTF of just 1,000 hours (~41 days). Redundancy is not optional at scale.



Three Core Techniques
Mirroring — every disk has an exact duplicate. Writes go to both; reads can come from either. Data is lost only if both disks in a pair fail before one is repaired — extremely unlikely.
Striping — data is split across multiple disks so reads/writes happen in parallel. Can be done at the bit, byte, or block level. Block-level striping is the standard used in most RAID levels.
Parity — an extra parity block computed via XOR. If one disk fails, its data can be reconstructed from the remaining disks and the parity. Much cheaper than mirroring since you don’t need to duplicate the entire disk.



Standard RAID Levels

RAID 0 — Block Striping
Data is striped across disks with no redundancy whatsoever.

✓ Best write performance of all RAID levels — no parity to update.
✓ 100% storage efficiency.
✗ No fault tolerance — one disk failure loses everything.
Use when: speed matters and data can be recovered from another source.




RAID 1 — Mirroring
Every disk has an exact copy on a second disk.

✓ Excellent fault tolerance — survives one disk failure.
✓ Reads can be served from either disk in parallel.
✗ 50% storage efficiency — half your disks are copies.
✗ Most expensive solution.
Use when: high-update workloads, OS drives, transaction databases.




RAID 2 — Bit Striping + Hamming Parity
Strips data at the bit level, uses Hamming codes for error correction.

Can correct one-bit errors and detect two-bit errors.
Requires multiple dedicated check disks.
✗ Not used in practice — subsumed by RAID 3.




RAID 3 — Byte Striping + Dedicated Parity
Strips at the byte level with a single dedicated parity disk.

✓ High data transfer rate — data accessed in parallel across all disks.
✗ Cannot service multiple requests simultaneously — every request touches every disk.
✗ Not used in practice — block striping (RAID 5) is more efficient.




RAID 4 — Block Striping + Dedicated Parity
Strips at the block level with a single dedicated parity disk.

✓ Read requests can be served by a single disk — better than RAID 3 for reads.
✓ Can recover from one disk failure using XOR.
✗ Write performance is poor — every write hits the single parity disk, creating a bottleneck.
✗ Not used in practice — RAID 5 distributes the parity bottleneck.




RAID 5 — Block Striping + Distributed Parity
Like RAID 4 but parity blocks are spread across all disks instead of sitting on one dedicated disk.

✓ Eliminates the parity bottleneck — multiple writes can happen in parallel.
✓ All disks participate in reads — higher read parallelism.
✓ Survives one disk failure.
✗ Single sector write: 2 reads + 2 writes (to update parity) — slower than RAID 1 for writes.
Use when: low-update workloads, large datasets, data warehouses, web servers.




RAID 6 — Block Striping + Double Distributed Parity
Extends RAID 5 with a second parity block, using Reed-Solomon codes.

✓ Survives two simultaneous disk failures — safe even during a rebuild after one failure.
✗ Write performance worse than RAID 5 — two parity blocks to update.
Rarely used — RAID 1 and RAID 5 are sufficient for most applications.





Hybrid RAID
Hybrid RAID combines two standard levels. Naming convention: left digit = lower layer, right digit = higher layer.

RAID 01 — Mirror of Stripes
Stripe sets are built first (RAID 0), then each set is mirrored (RAID 1).

If one disk in a stripe fails, the entire stripe set is lost — falls back to the mirror.
Less resilient than RAID 10.
Requires at least 4 disks. Storage efficiency: 50%.




RAID 10 — Stripe of Mirrors
Disks are mirrored first (RAID 1), then striped across the mirror pairs (RAID 0).

One disk in each mirror pair can fail independently — far more resilient than RAID 01.
Best throughput and latency of all fault-tolerant RAID levels.
Preferred for: databases, email servers, web servers, any I/O-intensive application.





Choosing a RAID Level



Use case
Recommended level




Speed only, data is disposable
RAID 0


High-update workloads (log disks, OS)
RAID 1


Low-update, large datasets
RAID 5


Two-disk failure tolerance required
RAID 6


Databases, file servers, max performance + safety
RAID 10




📌 RAID 1 writes faster than RAID 5 (2 writes vs 2 reads + 2 writes). As disk capacity grows and storage costs drop, RAID 1 is increasingly preferred even for large deployments.




What RAID Does NOT Do

❌ Replace backups — RAID protects against disk failure, not accidental deletion, corruption, or malware.
❌ Guarantee 100% uptime — RAID controllers themselves can fail.
❌ Protect against human error — a deleted file is deleted on all mirrors too.
❌ Allow easy capacity expansion — adding a disk usually requires rebuilding the array from scratch.
❌ Replace SAN solutions for virtualization and high-availability failover.


⚠️ RAID is one layer of a broader data protection strategy — it must always be combined with a proper backup plan.

text:
Three Core Techniques

Mirroring
Every disk has an exact duplicate — the logical disk consists of two physical disks.

Every write is carried out on both disks simultaneously.
Reads can be served from either disk.
If one disk in a pair fails, data is still available on the other.
Data loss only occurs if both disks in a pair fail before one is repaired — extremely unlikely.




Striping
Data is split across multiple disks so reads and writes happen in parallel.
Bit-level Striping

Bits of each byte are split across multiple disks (bit \(i\) goes to disk \(i\)).
Each access reads data at up to 8× the rate of a single disk.
Seek and access time is worse than a single disk — rarely used today.

Byte-level Striping

Each file is split into 1-byte chunks distributed across disks.
The \(i\)th byte goes to disk \(((i-1) \mod n) + 1\).

Block-level Striping

Block \(i\) of a file goes to disk \((i \mod n) + 1\).
Requests for different blocks can run in parallel if they reside on different disks.
A long sequential read can utilise all disks at once.




Parity
Parity provides fault tolerance by storing extra computed information alongside the data. If a disk fails, the lost data can be reconstructed from the remaining disks and the parity — without needing a full duplicate copy.
Parity is computed using XOR: for any set of bits, XOR of all bits including the parity bit equals zero. So if one disk’s bits are lost, XOR of the remaining disks recovers them.



XOR Gate


Bit-interleaved Parity

One parity bit covers the corresponding bits across all data disks.
Written to a dedicated parity disk on every write.

title: Backup and Recovery
text:
What is Backup and Recovery?
Imagine your database crashes due to a power failure. Without a backup, everything is gone. A backup is a copy of your database — data files, control files, logs — that lets you restore the system when something goes wrong.
Recovery is the process of using that backup to bring the database back to its last consistent state.

text:
Types of Data to Back Up

Business Data — includes personal information of clients, employees, contractors etc. along with details about places, things, events and rules related to the business.
System Data — includes specific environment/configuration of the system used for specialised development purposes log files, software dependency data, disk images.
Media Files — files like photographs, videos, sounds, graphics etc. need backing up. Media files are typically much larger in size.

text:

Full Backup
A full backup copies everything — tables, indexes, views, procedures. Think of it as a complete snapshot of the database at a point in time. It must be done at least once before any other strategy can be used.

Instead of copying everything, an incremental backup only copies what has changed since the last backup (full or incremental).







✓ Advantages
✗ Disadvantages

Recovery needs full + every incremental in sequence


Minimal downtime
Missing even one incremental breaks recovery


Most cost-efficient
Most complex to manage






Differential Backup
A differential backup copies everything that has changed since the last full backup — regardless of any incrementals in between. Recovery only ever needs two things: the last full backup and the most recent differential.
The longer you wait between differentials, the larger they grow — eventually approaching full backup size.

Larger than incremental backups

Hot Backup
All the strategies above are cold backups — the database pauses during the backup. But some systems can never go offline: financial trading platforms, real-time sensor systems, satellite feeds.
Hot backup keeps the database fully live while the backup runs concurrently.

text:
Transactional Logging with Hot Backup
During a hot backup, the database keeps running and changes keep happening. Every modification must be written to the transaction log first, then to the database.
If a crash occurs during a hot backup:

Recover — restore the last data backup (may be inconsistent) and the backed-up transaction log.
Restore — replay all transaction logs generated during the backup window to re-establish consistency.

The distinction between recover (getting the files back) and restore (making the database consistent again) is important — the database is only ready for users once both steps are done.

title: Log-Based Recovery
text:
The Recovery Algorithm (Concurrent Transactions)
With multiple transactions running at once, they share one buffer and one log. To keep recovery safe, uncommitted writes must not be visible to other transactions — enforced using exclusive locks held until commit or abort (strict two-phase locking).
Recovery runs in two phases:

Phase 1 — Redo Phase
Scan the log forward from the last checkpoint:

< Ti, Xj, V1, V2 > → write V2 to Xj.
< Ti start > → add Ti to the undo-list.
< Ti commit > or < Ti abort > → remove Ti from the undo-list.



Phase 2 — Undo Phase
Scan the log backwards until the undo-list is empty:

< Ti, Xj, V1, V2 > for Ti in undo-list → write V1 to Xj; write CLR < Ti, Xj, V1 >.
< Ti start > for Ti in undo-list → write < Ti abort >; remove Ti from undo-list.

text:
What is RAID?
A single disk has two problems: it’s slow, and it can fail. RAID solves both by combining multiple disks into what looks like one — spreading data across them for speed and duplicating it for safety. RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) is a disk organization technique that manages multiple disks and presents them as a single logical disk. It achieves two things simultaneously:

title: RAID: Redundant Array of Independent Disks
text:
Three Core Techniques

Mirroring
Every disk has an exact duplicate — the logical disk consists of two physical disks.

Every write is carried out on both disks simultaneously.
Reads can be served from either disk.
If one disk in a pair fails, data is still available on the other.
Data loss only occurs if both disks in a pair fail before one is repaired — extremely unlikely.




Striping
Data is split across multiple disks so reads and writes happen in parallel.
Bit-level Striping

Bits of each byte are split across multiple disks (bit \(i\) goes to disk \(i\)).
Each access reads data at up to 8× the rate of a single disk.
Seek and access time is worse than a single disk — rarely used today.

Byte-level Striping

Each file is split into 1-byte chunks distributed across disks.
The \(i\)th byte goes to disk \(((i-1) \mod n) + 1\).

Block-level Striping

Block \(i\) of a file goes to disk \((i \mod n) + 1\).
Requests for different blocks can run in parallel if they reside on different disks.
A long sequential read can utilise all disks at once.




Parity
Parity provides fault tolerance by storing extra computed information alongside the data. If a disk fails, the lost data can be reconstructed from the remaining disks and the parity — without needing a full duplicate copy.
Parity is computed using XOR: for any set of bits, XOR of all bits including the parity bit equals zero. So if one disk’s bits are lost, XOR of the remaining disks recovers them.



XOR Gate


Bit-interleaved Parity

One parity bit covers the corresponding bits across all data disks.
Written to a dedicated parity disk on every write.
On disk failure: XOR all remaining bits (including parity) to reconstruct the lost bit.

Block-interleaved Parity

Uses block-level striping with a dedicated parity block (not just a bit) for every set of corresponding blocks across \(n\) disks.
On disk failure: XOR the corresponding blocks from all remaining disks to reconstruct the lost block.

title: Query Optimization and Equivalence
text:
Equivalence Rules
How does the database optimizer know that two different execution plans will return the exact same result? It relies on Equivalence Rules.
These mathematical rules state that certain relational algebra expressions can be transformed into other expressions without changing the final output. The optimizer applies these rules to rewrite the query into a more efficient form.

1. Selection Rules

Conjunctive selections can be split: A selection with multiple conditions connected by AND (\(\land\)) can be broken down into a sequence of individual selections. \[ \sigma_{\theta_1 \land \theta_2}(E) = \sigma_{\theta_1}(\sigma_{\theta_2}(E)) \]
Selections are commutative: The order in which you apply filters doesn’t matter. \[ \sigma_{\theta_1}(\sigma_{\theta_2}(E)) = \sigma_{\theta_2}(\sigma_{\theta_1}(E)) \]



2. Projection Rules

Only the final projection matters: In a sequence of projection operations, only the last one is necessary; the others can be safely omitted. \[ \Pi_{L_1}(\Pi_{L_2}(...\Pi_{L_n}(E)))) = \Pi_{L_1}(E) \]



3. Join Rules

Theta-joins are commutative: Joining Table A to Table B gives the same result as joining Table B to Table A. \[ E_1 \bowtie_\theta E_2 = E_2 \bowtie_\theta E_1 \]
Natural joins are associative: When joining three tables, it doesn’t matter which two you join first. \[ (E_1 \bowtie E_2) \bowtie E_3 = E_1 \bowtie (E_2 \bowtie E_3) \]
Selections can be combined with Cartesian products to form a join: \[ \sigma_{\theta}(E1 \times E2) = E_1 \bowtie_\theta E_2 \]
Selections can be absorbed into a join condition: \[ \sigma_{\theta_1}(E_1 \bowtie_{\theta_2} E_2) = E_1 \bowtie_{\theta_1 \land \theta_2 } E_2 \]



4. Set Operation Rules

Associative:

Union: \((E_1 \cup E_2) \cup E_3 = E_1 \cup (E_2 \cup E_3)\)
Intersection: \((E_1 \cap E_2) \cap E_3 = E_1 \cap (E_2 \cap E_3)\)

Commutative:

Union: \(E_1 \cup E_2 = E_2 \cup E_1\)
Intersection: \(E_1 \cap E_2 = E_2 \cap E_1\)
(Note: Set difference is NOT commutative)

Projection distributes over union: \[ \Pi_L(E_1 \cup E_2) = (\Pi_L(E_1)) \cup (\Pi_L(E_2)) \]

title: Query Processing and Cost
text:
Overview of Query Processing
When you submit a query to a database, it doesn’t just execute it directly. It goes through a series of logical steps to ensure the query is valid and to find the most efficient way to execute it.
The process can be broken down into three main phases:

title: Query Processing and Cost
text:
The phases of query processing.




1. Parser and Translator

What it does: The database receives the raw SQL query. It checks the syntax to ensure it’s valid SQL, and verifies that the referenced tables and columns exist in the database schema.
Output: It translates the query into an internal format, typically a relational algebra expression.



2. Optimization

What it does: This is the most crucial step for performance. A single SQL query can often be executed in multiple ways (e.g., different join orders, using an index vs. scanning a table).
The Optimizer’s Job: It analyzes these different strategies (execution plans), estimates the cost of each using available database statistics, and selects the one with the lowest overall cost.



3. Evaluation

What it does: The query-execution engine takes the optimized query-evaluation plan and actually runs it against the data.
Output: It returns the final result set (the answers) to the user.

title: Query Processing and Cost
text:
Measures of Query Cost
How does the optimizer determine the “cost” of a query plan?
The true cost is generally measured as the total elapsed time required to answer the query. This involves several factors:

Disk accesses (reading/writing data from/to storage)
CPU time (processing the data)
Network communication (if data is distributed)

However, because fetching data from disk is typically the slowest operation by a huge margin, we simplify the cost measure to focus primarily on disk I/O.
We measure cost using two main metrics:

Number of block transfers (\(b\)): The number of data blocks that must be read from or written to the disk.
Number of seeks (\(S\)): The number of times the disk head must move to a new location to read a block.


The Cost Formula
We can estimate the time cost with this simple formula:
\[ \text{Cost} = (b \times t_T) + (S \times t_S) \]
Where:

\(b\) = Total number of block transfers
\(t_T\) = Time to transfer one block
\(S\) = Total number of seeks
\(t_S\) = Time for one seek

title: Join Algorithms
text:
Understanding Join Costs
Joining tables is one of the most common and resource-intensive operations in a database. Therefore, optimizing how a join is executed is critical.
Let’s look at three fundamental algorithms for performing joins and how their costs are calculated.
Terminology: When joining two relations (tables), \(r\) and \(s\):

title: Join Algorithms
text:
1. Nested Loop Join
This is the simplest and most naive join algorithm. It uses two nested for loops.
Analogy: Imagine having two physical phone books. For every single person in Book A, you flip through the entire Book B page-by-page to find a matching name. Very tedious!
How it works: For every single tuple in the outer relation \(r\), it scans through every single tuple in the inner relation \(s\) to find a match.
for each tuple tr in r do
    for each tuple ts in s do
        if tr and ts match the join condition then
            add (tr, ts) to the result
Cost:

Block Transfers: \(n_r \times b_s + b_r\) (For each of the \(n_r\) tuples, it reads all \(b_s\) blocks of the inner relation, plus the initial \(b_r\) blocks of the outer relation).
Seeks: \(n_r + b_r\)

title: Join Algorithms
text:
2. Block Nested Loop Join
This algorithm is a major improvement over the standard nested loop join. Instead of looping tuple-by-tuple, it processes the data block-by-block.
Analogy: Instead of looking up one person at a time, you tear out a whole page of names from Book A, memorize them, and then flip through Book B looking for matches for anyone on your memorized page.
How it works: For every block in the outer relation \(r\), it scans every block in the inner relation \(s\). It then joins the tuples within those loaded blocks in memory. This drastically reduces the number of times the inner table has to be read from disk.
for each block Br in r do
    for each block Bs in s do
        for each tuple tr in Br do
            for each tuple ts in Bs do
                if tr and ts match then
                    add (tr, ts) to the result
Cost:

Block Transfers: \(b_r \times b_s + b_r\) (For each of the \(b_r\) blocks, it reads all \(b_s\) blocks of the inner relation, plus the initial \(b_r\) blocks).
Seeks: \(2 \times b_r\)

Cost using Nested Loop Join
Using student as the outer relation (\(r\)):

Block Transfers: \(5000 \times 400 + 100 = 2,000,100\)
Seeks: \(5000 + 100 = 5,100\)



Cost using Block Nested Loop Join
Using student as the outer relation (\(r\)):

Block Transfers: \(100 \times 400 + 100 = 40,100\)
Seeks: \(2 \times 100 = 200\)



Cost using Indexed Nested-Loop Join
Imagine takes has a B+-tree index on the attribute ID. The height of the tree is 4, plus one access to find the actual data, so \(c \approx 5\) accesses per lookup. Using student as the outer relation (\(r\)):

Cost (in block transfers and seeks): \(100 + (5000 \times 5) = 25,100\)

Conclusion:

The Block Nested Loop Join (40,100 transfers) is drastically more efficient than the basic nested loop (2 million transfers) because it reads data in chunks.
The Indexed Nested-Loop Join (25,100 accesses) is even faster because it completely avoids scanning the takes table, jumping directly to the correct records using the index!

title: Join Algorithms
text:
3. Indexed Nested-Loop Join
This algorithm makes use of existing indexes to completely skip scanning the inner relation.
Analogy: Instead of flipping through Book B blindly, you use the alphabetized index at the back of Book B to jump exactly to the page containing the name you’re looking for from Book A.
How it works: If the inner relation \(s\) has an index on the join attribute, the database can use it. For each tuple \(t_r\) in the outer relation \(r\), it simply performs an index lookup on \(s\) to instantly find the matching tuples.
Cost:

Cost of the join: \(b_r \times (t_T + t_S) + n_r \times c\)

Where \(c\) is the cost of traversing the index and fetching all matching \(s\) tuples for one tuple in \(r\).

Best Practice: If both relations have an index, the database optimizer will choose the relation with fewer tuples as the outer relation (\(r\)) to minimize the number of index lookups.

What do Database Applications Need?
When building data-intensive applications, you need a database that performs well under pressure. Performance is judged by three main metrics:

text:
Throughput: Transactions per second (tps). Think of this as the number of cars passing through a toll booth every minute.
Response Time: The delay from submitting a query to getting the result. Think of this as how long one specific car waits in line.
Availability: Mean time to failure. How often is the toll booth open and working without breaking down?

title: Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data
text:
RDBMS Architecture
Historically, relational databases (RDBMS) have been built using different architectures depending on the scale of the organization.

1. Centralized Systems
Run on a single machine (like a desktop or a single server) and do not interact with other computers.

Analogy: Keeping all your company’s files in a single filing cabinet in one office.



2. Client-Server Systems
The work is divided. Client machines handle the front-end (user interface, forms), while a powerful Server machine handles the back-end (query evaluation, transaction management, data storage).

Analogy: A restaurant. The waiters (Clients) take the orders from the customers and pass them to the kitchen (Server), which does the heavy lifting of cooking the food.



3. Parallel Systems
Uses multiple processors and disks connected by a fast internal network. It aims for two things:

Speedup: Making a single big task run faster.
Scaleup: Handling a larger workload without slowing down.



4. Distributed Systems
Data is spread across multiple separate machines (nodes) connected via a network (like the internet).

Advantages: Data can be shared globally, and if one node fails, others can keep the system running (high availability).
crumbs: 43  Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data

title: Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data
text:
Scaling Databases: Horizontal vs. Vertical
When your application gets popular (like a viral social media app), your single database server will eventually hit its limit. You have two choices for scaling:

Vertical Scaling (Scaling Up)
This means adding more resources (CPU, RAM, faster disks) to your existing single machine.

Analogy: You need to transport more boxes. Vertical scaling is taking your pickup truck to the mechanic and upgrading it into a massive 18-wheeler semi-truck.
Pros: Cost-effective at first, less complex, no need to change your software.
Cons: There is a physical limit to how big one machine can get. Eventually, you can’t buy a bigger truck.



Horizontal Scaling (Scaling Out)
This means adding additional machines (nodes) to your infrastructure to share the load.

Analogy: You need to transport more boxes. Horizontal scaling is buying a fleet of 10 normal pickup trucks instead of one massive semi-truck.
Pros: Virtually infinite scaling, increased resilience (if one truck breaks down, you have 9 others).
Cons: Much more complex. You now have to coordinate a whole fleet instead of driving just one vehicle.

title: Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data
text:
The Rise of Big Data
Relational databases are fantastic, but the explosion of web applications, social media, and IoT devices generated a “perfect storm” of data that traditional RDBMS systems struggled to handle.
This is the era of Big Data, characterized by the 5 V’s:

Volume: Massive quantities of data (Terabytes to Exabytes).
Velocity: Data generated at lightning speed, often requiring real-time processing.
Variety: Data isn’t just neat tables anymore. It’s unstructured text, images, videos, and sensor logs.
Variability: Inconsistent data flows.
Veracity: Varying data quality and accuracy.

title: Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data
text:
The CAP Theorem
When you use Horizontal Scaling to build a distributed database system across multiple nodes, you run into the CAP Theorem.
The theorem states that a distributed system can only guarantee two out of the following three properties at any given time:

Consistency (C): All clients see the exact same data at the same time, no matter which node they connect to.
Availability (A): The system always accepts reads and writes, even if some nodes fail.
Partition Tolerance (P): The system continues to operate even if a network failure cuts off communication between some nodes.

The ATM Analogy: Imagine two ATMs (nodes) connected to a central bank. Suddenly, the network cable is cut (a Partition).

Do you let a user withdraw money anyway, risking that they might withdraw the same funds at the other ATM? (Choosing Availability over Consistency).
Or do you freeze the ATMs and show an “Out of Service” error until the network is fixed, ensuring no accounts are overdrawn? (Choosing Consistency over Availability).

In the world of Big Data, network partitions are inevitable. Therefore, modern systems usually have to choose between Consistency and Availability.

title: Architecture, Scaling, and Big Data
text:
Enter NoSQL
Because RDBMS systems rigidly enforce Consistency (ACID properties), they struggle to scale horizontally for massive, high-velocity web apps.
This led to NoSQL (Not Only SQL) databases. They drop strict relational rules in favor of massive scalability, often choosing Availability over strong Consistency (relying instead on Eventual Consistency).

Types of NoSQL Databases

Key-Value Stores (e.g., DynamoDB, Redis)

Acts like a massive dictionary. You look up a “Key” and get a “Value”. Extremely fast for simple data.
Example: Storing user session data or shopping cart contents.

Document Stores (e.g., MongoDB, CouchDB)

Stores data in flexible, JSON-like documents. Great for hierarchical or deeply nested data.
Example: Content management systems, personalization engines.

Column-Oriented Stores (e.g., Cassandra, HBase)

Stores data in columns rather than rows. Excellent for searching and aggregating massive datasets.
Example: Logging user clicks on a massive e-commerce website.

Graph Databases (e.g., Neo4j)

Designed to store and navigate relationships (nodes and edges) rather than tables.
Example: Social networks. Finding “Friends of friends who like Pizza” is instantly resolved by walking the graph, whereas an RDBMS would require painfully slow, complex table joins.
